comment_evidence.clause: too much visual clutter and in general the map layout gets worse the more you play the game as they use the teleporters as a crutch which you probably dont have access to anyways
comment_evidence.full_review:
This game was very fun. The atmosphere and map *visual* design is outstanding and is leaps and bounds above SL1. I also enjoyed the change from using extractors for resources to finding them around the map and them making chickens an actually viable option for ranching rather than being stuck entirely to veggies or fruit (albeit this was required as they removed the Rad, tangle (meat), mosaic and quantum slimes and added more meat/nectar eaters than fruit/veg eaters.)
The core gameplay was made easier with the bee drones allowing for automation, the coops autoplucking the elderly and the like.

However, the map layout was quite frankly abhorrent once you got to the endgame area, constant backtracking to get plorts from the other side of the map or your ranch. You likely dont have multiple two way teleporters at this point unless you played really slow and chances are you are using the two way teleporters you do have getting to the endgame area (since the built in shortcut to this place is basically at the end of the game) not using them between the map. (assuming you actually want to use the diamonds on them to begin with and not for the drones).
And most of these just unlock shortcuts you dont need, but you cant tell this until you open half of them.
This is ontop of the fact that after all these plort backtracking, when you do get to the final area. The game tells you to backtrack all over again to find special "doors" you can open. If you god forbid didnt remember the locations of all of these, have fun re-exploring the nightmare zone again.

After a certain point in the game I completely ignored my ranch, which felt kind of antithetical to the idea of playing a game called Slime rancher. The ranch was running itself and tbh by the point I was making the drones it didnt feel like I needed money anymore and it was more just because the game is called slime rancher that i bothered to keep up with it.

Another major issue with the endgame zone is the wandering event, it is painful to look at depending on the area you are in. Sometimes it looks amazing, sometimes its just mass visual clutter with way too many moving textures in a game with a lot of movement on screen already.

TLDR: area's look amazing and the gameplay is just SL1 but more refined.  too much backtracking, too much visual clutter and in general the map layout gets worse the more you play the game as they use the teleporters as a crutch which you probably dont have access to anyways.
This game is positive solely because for most of the backtracking i didnt mind because i liked looking at the world, but it was definitely getting to me at the end.

comment_evidence.clause: Sound effects are good but audio in general is maybe a little on the LOUD side lol Obviously that can be tamed in the settings so it loses no points there
comment_evidence.full_review:
So far so good! Never expected to enjoy this one as much having assumed, wrongly, that it would be much like many other "tower" games that I have tried and not enjoyed. 
 
I took the risk and have been pleasantly surprised. 
 
Gameplay is surprisingly fast-paced, even chaotic at times. Which makes sense given the chaotic nature of journalism. The pause button becomes a strong ally in no time to let you gather your thoughts and arrange your articles before time runs out! 
 
The UI is organised, dynamic and well illustrated and the soundtrack is period and lively. Sound effects are good but audio in general is maybe a little on the LOUD side lol Obviously that can be tamed in the settings so it loses no points there. 
 
Progression is nice too, steady and has a few different avenues you can take depending on which direction you fancy taking your Newspaper.  
All in all a solid game especially considering the price point which is extremely justified

For an early access game, it already feel pretty polished. The gameplay loop is solid, the graphics is charming and the music is very groovy (I like how the background music and the end of week result music uses the same motif). 
 
A few things I'd like to see: 
- More furniture in general. 
- More wallpaper design. Currently the set of wallpapers serve specific uses but there's little variety in them. I want to see more set of wallpapers that grant similar bonuses so players can choose between one or the other designs. 
- Make The Mayor, The Mafia and High Society more gameplay relevant. Currently they serve as quests giver to the player every week, but other than that they don't provide any other effects. It'd be nice to see if they could interact with each other or have an effect on the long term gameplay (perhaps at some point once you hit the midgame?). I think there's a lot of potential to be have here. 
 
Other than that I look forward to what this game is going to be like at full release.

comment_evidence.clause: The build menu is a little clunky to navigate and it took me ages to figure out how to click out of the map screen
comment_evidence.full_review:
Really fun & addictive management sim with an immersive gameplay loop and a great 1930s New York vibe. The fact it's this smooth & fleshed out in early access is very promising, excited to see what they do with it.

Stuff I loved:
- The gameplay blend of designing your building, managing your employees moods and refining your story production line is top notch.
- Constructing the layout of each week's issue and trying to find the best story combos is a really fun puzzle element.
- The satisfaction of pulling the lever to run the issue each week then watching the animation of the print press running through my tower was like crack.
- The coziness of the soundtrack. The blend of office sound effects, rain, traffic noise and jazz is awesome.

A few small things I would love to see improved:
- A greater variety of stories so you're not forced to print the same headline 7-8 times in a game run. Even if it's just some re-skins of existing stories with different words in the headline.
- Some more incentive to actually read the headlines you print. I found late in the game I was purely looking at the tags on the stories I chose instead of reading the words I was actually printing in my newspaper because they didn't matter. Maybe if there was a penalty for printing a typo or printing a headline you already ran in a previous issue, or perhaps a bonus for printing a meaningful follow-up to a story you printed in the last issue, that would make the player actually have to read & engage with the stories more. Could provide some Papers Please style concentration to the game.
- A few extra tracks in the already great soundtrack. There's a couple songs which sound more 1950s than 1930s but that's a minor gripe.
- A few UI tweaks are needed. The build menu is a little clunky to navigate and it took me ages to figure out how to click out of the map screen. I liked the detail that each story in the research screen takes place in a different real-life city with accurate city layout in the story screen, but the story UI would always hide the name of each city whenever it opens!
- Seasons would be cool, would love to see snow in the winter.

I found this to be a nice single player completionist game where I felt able to complete all the achievements and goals without the need to google anything, so I got a nice sense of completion at the end. It also feels like a nice game to come back to every now and again just to run around in and smash some flower pots because the graphics are sooo nice and generally lag friendly. :) Thank you for an amazing game!!!

comment_evidence.clause: sprinting and clipping a wall (or sometimes the air) results in fully losing your momentum and bouncing back with a stun animation that is cute the first few times
comment_evidence.full_review:
Given my two options for a review, I feel more positive than negative about Little Kitty Big City, but the game has some notable issues a prospective player should know. Firstly, my positives: the game seems to do all it set out to do; it is a light, fluffy game about playing as a cat. It is a third-person sandbox platformer (with notable goat simulator inspiration) with some mildly funny dialog and characters. The art style works well for the tone and is consistently nice to look at (witness the kitty, for they are adorable). I also want to commend whoever did the camera, as it worked fantastically with almost no issues throughout my entire playtime. 
 
The most important negative is that the traversal feels terrible to me. The traversal system is based on a charged and aimed jump that ends up feeling super clunky and is combined with a BOTW/TOTK style climbing system (the climbing is fine, but it feels super slow). On top of this, sprinting and clipping a wall (or sometimes the air) results in fully losing your momentum and bouncing back with a stun animation that is cute the first few times, but quickly gets annoying when you are just trying to get around. 
 
Overall, I would say not to expect anything revolutionary, but I had a somewhat positive time and was able to 100% it (with some frankly tedious grinding) in a weekend.

comment_evidence.clause: aside from some outdated graphics on the store page and the issues I explained previously
comment_evidence.full_review:
I really liked this game! It's adorable, well animated, well written, and the environmental design is excellent. It could have been my new favorite game on Steam, but it has a few problems holding it back. Despite following the game's development from before release, I didn't have the budget to get it until now. That said, I can't know if it's always been this way, but I experienced glitches every time I played it, and I could even recreate the more memorable ones. This surprised me, because the game just got a few holiday themed updates in December, so I'm not sure how the game has stayed this unstable.

My most frequent problem was often I struggled to use the newer features in the game, such as the extra menu options for cosmetics and photo mode, with only my controller. The game gives a pop up at the very beginning, recommending a controller, but you can't exit photo mode without the keyboard, and you can't cycle into new menus for extra hats in the pause menu. I don't know how the Switch version handles this, if it even got the same updates. There's no options in the settings to adjust your keybinds for these newer features either, so it's not a problem I can fix myself.

I experienced many glitches, including warping across the map during normal gameplay, even into out of bounds. At one point my camera was locked in place. I've been able to recreate this one, I pulled a traffic cone onto a little rock and it promptly got stuck hovering 3 feet in the air. I once had an issue where I couldn't pounce on birds anymore, the slow-motion effect halved how far I should have gone, causing me to fall short of every pounce. Most of these I fixed by warping away through the sewer fast travel, or by restarting the application.

Despite all my issues, I completed the game 100% in 11 hours, purely from passion, and because it's quite easy to do. If you know what you're doing you could finish it even faster. The platforming and movement is a little awkward, it's not going to wow you, but it's designed well enough that you can get used to the quirks and move competently, if not gracefully. The characters are charming, the dialogue is fun and well written, and everyone is very polite and emotionally mature, or tries their best to be. It's an excellent example to younger players. 

However, while the game looks very kid-friendly, I would recommend parental supervision. A child who can't read will struggle with achieving goals in the game, and could easily become stuck. Especially if he or she activates photo mode and doesn't have access to the keyboard. If your child can read, you can be very hands off as long as you can trust your child at a computer. However, I recommend supervision during a specific quest. The first time you meet a beetle, she will speak in online lingo, and specifically explains what "LOL" means. Beetle then goes on to use LM*O once, without explaining what it means, and it's possible your child will either look it up or ask you about its meaning. While you could tell your child to ignore Beetle entirely, this means many other quests are inaccessible and you would have to have some way to enforce it. Another point of distress for you or your child is that Kitty can fall from very high up. You must climb multiple tall buildings, and if Kitty falls from a great height, there's no harm done in the game, and Kitty recovers quickly, but the flailing animation on the way down and the smack sound effect on impact could trouble sensitive players. One thing that may help is that the game starts with Kitty falling from its perch on a tall building and having a dramatic but comedic fall, so it's likely that falling will have already been associated with an OK outcome from the beginning.

Overall, aside from some outdated graphics on the store page and the issues I explained previously, I got exactly what I came for when I played this game, and I had a good time. I recommend it if you don't mind a bit of a messy experience sometimes. I didn't get anything game-breaking, but with how all the items in the game stay in the places you left them, I'm guessing it's quite possible something vital to game completion could get stuck out of bounds forever. I think if the game is tweaked a bit to fix the bugs, and if the movement is refined even further, (and I dare to hope for a truly child-friendly dialogue change,) Little Kitty, Big City could become one of my favorite games.

comment_evidence.clause: There's no big bad - the main antagonist is the environment you need to navigate
comment_evidence.full_review:
Little Kitty Big City (LKBC) is a fun little game. The plot is that you're a cat trying to get back to your owner, who lives in the highest room in the tallest tower. There's a light story along the way with flat but fun characters. There's no big bad - the main antagonist is the environment you need to navigate. It's cozy and relaxing.

Your cat controls fairly smooth. You can run, jump, pounce, nap, loaf, purr, and other cat things. Platforming can get difficult as aiming and timing can be clunky. This is an issue with all platformers, but LKBC suffers especially because it's one of the few places where your feeling of being a cat gets thrown off. You can't be as nimble as a cat, often.

The art style fits with the laid-back cozy nature of the game. The city is a pleasure to walk through while the character designs are okay. The humans are pretty bland. That might fit if you are into the art theory that a cat would not particularly care what a person looks like. 

My main complaint is that the game can be nearly 100% in 5-6 hours. I completed most of the side-quests and unlocked a bunch in four hours and I wasn't trying to speed run. I spent a lot of time goofing around chewing the scenery and tripping humans for giggles. I have a 9 to 5 job, and I do non-game things, and yet I still got through the main quest in two days. 

Overall? Good fun, loved the style. Just be aware that most of the ride will depend on how long you want to be unbothered. Moisturized. In your lane. Thriving. As a cat.

The art style is amazing very much inspired by silent hill ps1 but it also feels like a modern take on that style with the free camera and non pre rendered backgrounds that feel pre rendered if that makes sense.

Puzzles are challenging but not too obtuse.

Story is very interesting and engaging!

And most of all it’s horrifying!!!

comment_evidence.full_review:
An absolutely fantastic survival horror that rocks old school graphics. Everything about this game from start to finish was a treat of seeing a beautifully crafted world that fully embraced being a cheery theme park even in a dilapidated state with the various areas and puzzled perfectly feeling like something straight out of a park. The music gave me a good chuckle here and there with how it created nostalgia in with cheerful tunes or shrink into my seat when it cut down to silence or a low drone. The atmosphere was perfectly crafted for creating a sense of safety when needed but also putting you on the edge of your seat, be that with low tones or distinct lack of sound.  
 
Puzzles are fun in the itches your brain good way, nothing too crazy but nothing underwhelming, it always grants a feeling of satisfaction once you figure it out. The enemy types trickle in as the story goes onward without any big announcement, they just show up and leave you trying to figure out what their quirk is and how easily you can deal with them or if their best left alone. Even if you do leave enemies the game doesn't make an area impossible to get through as more trickle in, it just requires a bit of wit and a lot of praying to squeak through a clump of enemies without taking too much damage. 
 
On the horror side of things this game kept it well done even when I was in the end game portion. I never felt 100% on top of the enemies or could zone out in an area, I kept feeling on my toes ready to bolt when something got unnerving. With the gradual enemy trickle, and some unique encounters tucked away here and there, coming out of a safe room to something I didn't recognize immediately put the fear right back to the front of my mind. There were several times I dropped my guard doing a puzzle, or during brief lulls where I was figuring out my next point to go to, that took a bit of thought only to jump out of my chair moments later from something as small as a trap. Scares didn't feel cheap in the slightest, they all got my to fairly jump and some were because I wasn't paying attention to something I previously noted which was both funny and a reminder of how good the environment could make a trap you already saw blend right in, 
 
Overall I adored this game, it was an utter treat to go through for both the horror and the story. I'm aware I haven't said anything about the story yet, all you need to know is its good and taking the time to unravel it and make theories is part of the fun of this game. Crow Country is charming, unique, and perfectly frightening in all the right ways a survival horror game can be especially for one that takes a page out of the retro style.

comment_evidence.clause: And no awful "PS1-inspired" visual style—smothering the screen in post-processing effects to hide how ugly the game actually is—will ever substitute for the tension and suspense that should emerge through gameplay
comment_evidence.full_review:
I've played this on another platform before, and while I found it somewhat mediocre, I figured it deserved a second chance after picking it up on a good sale.

And... nah. As the kids like to say these days, it's a painfully [i]overrated[/i] game.

My cynicism toward the industry—especially the indie scene, which has been churning out industrial quantities of garbage for years now—has long since robbed me of any patience for swallowing creatively bankrupt, generic copies of games I played decades ago, with not the slightest hint of originality in sight, pretending to be something new—or even a competent recreation of the formula they're ripping off.

[i]Crow Country[/i] is just a generic [i]Resident Evil[/i] clone with a flat map and an isometric camera.

The theme park has its charm, some of the puzzles are enjoyable, and the developers at least have enough self-awareness to inject some humor into the experience. But the game's core design is executed so poorly that, throughout most of my playthrough, the only thing on my mind was that I'd rather just replay [i]Resident Evil[/i].

Combat and resource management are pointless.

On Normal difficulty, you'll drown in so many resources that you might not even notice how clumsily most of the game's mechanics are implemented.

There's no thought put into enemy placement, and avoiding them is trivial because most environments are so wide open and the enemies themselves are mostly harmless.

There is no synergy between the enemies and the level design. While they feature varied designs, they lack distinct behaviors. This is likely why any of them can be placed anywhere, yet the result always feels like the same generic encounter.

At no point in the entire game will you feel even the slightest bit apprehensive about encountering any enemy. Veeeery rarely will you have to make the strategic decision to eliminate an enemy blocking your path and spend resources, or weigh the risks of avoiding it instead. Most of the time, the answer is so obvious and so risk-free that the game never manages to create any tension.

As if that weren't enough, defeated enemies respawn. Worse still, brand-new environmental traps simply materialize in rooms you've already cleared, in a half-hearted attempt to force the player to be a little more careful. It only cheapens everything you do even further.

You can disarm a trap or kill a particularly noteworthy enemy, only for new ones to appear in their place.

Resources, however, do [i]not[/i] respawn. In fact, the game encourages you to waste your "precious" ammunition shooting crates—since you don't even have a melee weapon to break them—in the hope of getting random supplies. If you're already carrying the maximum amount of a particular resource, those items are simply forced onto the floor, where they'll disappear the moment you leave the room. 

Naturally, the crate doesn't come back either.

At least the game has the courtesy to let you return and pick up items that were already placed in the environment. Thank you, sir.

But none of this matters, because the consequences of wasting or losing resources are completely trivialized given the enormous amount the game showers you with.

Before i even found my second weapon, my inventory was already overflowing with ammunition for it. Likewise, i was carrying a mountain of healing items that I almost never had to use.

Suddenly it becomes obvious why the game never asks you to make genuinely difficult decisions. It also makes perfect sense that there's no inventory management or storage box. The balancing would completely fall apart.

The classic survival horror formula was elegant because every system reinforced the others. Every enemy represented an obstacle that presented meaningful choices with immediate consequences. The permanence of your actions was what gave weight to every other decision. Carefully designed enemy encounters forced you to choose. Avoiding threats with tank controls and fixed camera angles was a skill you had to develop, and it always came with the inherent risk of making a tiny mistake and potentially spending even more resources than if you'd taken the safer approach.

Crow Country suffers from a lack of permanence in almost everything you do—except the things that punish you. It tries to paper over the problem with an overabundance of resources, further undermining any sense of survival.

The result is that combat, resource management, and methodical exploration all feel completely pointless.

It's a horror game without a single drop of atmosphere. And no awful "PS1-inspired" visual style—smothering the screen in post-processing effects to hide how ugly the game actually is—will ever substitute for the tension and suspense that should emerge through gameplay.

Then there's the baffling addition of a free-aim system that contributes absolutely nothing to the game. There's a localized damage mechanic that apparently rewards headshots, but in practice it accomplishes nothing interesting beyond adding an awkward extra step to arrive at the exact same place as the games it's copying.

Not to mention the terrible controls and awful mouse support. Trying to use an aiming system designed for an over-the-shoulder third-person shooter in an isometric game simply doesn't work. Aiming is so sluggish and stiff that, most of the time, you won't have enough time to make any tactical decision before getting hit.

Waiting for enemies to get close enough before firing is simply a bad idea—one you almost never have to make anyway, because you almost never have to meaningfully engage with enemies in the first place.

And I suspect the developers knew how miserable this felt, because they conveniently scattered explosive barrels and similar hazards everywhere, allowing you to bypass the more dangerous enemies. Which, once again, is mostly pointless because they'll either respawn or are ridiculously easy to avoid.

If you think they at least took advantage of the free-aim mechanic to make the environments more interactive, prepare to be disappointed. 99%  of the time, shooting anything that isn't explicitly tied to a puzzle accomplishes absolutely nothing. I never found a single alternative solution through experimentation. I wasted plenty of bullets figuring that out—which ultimately didn't matter because of everything I've already mentioned.

On [i]Murder of Crows[/i] (Hard), all of these flaws become even more obvious. This time, the game pairs all of those irritating design decisions with a genuine scarcity of resources, making every decision that already lacked lasting consequences feel even more nonsensical.

Suddenly, those crates the game wants me to shoot become even more pointless. Everything that could be overlooked because of the overwhelming abundance of supplies turns into a genuine annoyance. Not the kind that enhances the experience, either. It just makes the whole game feel even more poorly planned.

Yeah... it's mediocre. Unpolished. Poorly thought out. A sloppy imitation of something the developers neither understood nor managed to reproduce competently. It has a certain nostalgic charm, and it's functional enough to avoid being outright broken, but it brings nothing new to the table, doesn't subvert any clichés, and isn't even a meaningful refinement of an old formula.

A game with no lasting appeal whatsoever. Its ideas are nothing more than poorly executed regurgitations of concepts that were already done thirty years ago—and they absolutely do not hold up under even the slightest scrutiny.

So that's [i]Crow Country[/i].

No joke—between the classic Resident Evil games and the many, many titles that cemented, refined, or explored the genre's creative possibilities, there are easily at least 30 better games I’d recommend over this one without a second thought.

Just grab an emulator and dive into the genre's classics; you’ll be much better off.

comment_evidence.clause: io "PSX horror" that is messy crt shaders over low poly models that don't have a solid grasp on what they're pulling from and often fall flat) I was gently dissuaded by Crow Country's aesthetic
comment_evidence.full_review:
I held off on this game for a while because I knew it was going to be a solid and cozy short survival horror game when I played the demo. I went in blind and I wound up liking it so much more than I would have expected! 
 
Coming off of the launch of Signalis, a game that is visually scary and explores its horror and themes in some surreal and interesting ways that really felt like a proper love letter to classic survival horror games (as opposed to the modern wave of itch.io "PSX horror" that is messy crt shaders over low poly models that don't have a solid grasp on what they're pulling from and often fall flat) I was gently dissuaded by Crow Country's aesthetic. It felt like it was pulling from an old-school visual aesthetic that didn't really exist, with bulbous character and enemy models and a grainy filter to emulate crunchy old graphics, and while I have definitely grown to love a lot of the style and personality the game has doing its own thing,  
 
I think Crow Country's strong points, especially aesthetically, come moreso from its great execution of fun ideas and the very palpable love for details. We finally have an awesome, succinct but dense survival horror set in a theme park and it is crafted with so much love in all of the little details, it oozes with all the charm and secret nooks and crannies of the best pre-rendered PSX backgrounds, and it is so delightful! The music and sounds are wonderful, puzzles usually have fairly simple solutions, but almost always have such creative and fun designs it doesn't matter, and I think that's a running theme for the game. Some of the "retro" aspects feel lacking or undercooked (shooting is both slippery and clunky in being intentionally obtuse and not super satisfying, plus the one handed firing animations for everything feels a little jarring. I'm also a freak who loves OG Silent Hill and RE combat so I'm a little more nitpicky on this) but the charm and cute little secrets and density of details in a game that doesn't overstay its welcome more than make up for all of this. 
 
For all of Crow Country's heavy handed and sometimes misguided attempts to recapture "old-school" survival horror, I think what surprised me most was how much fun I had with the story and atmosphere. It's a little hard to articulate, but I don't mean the visual atmosphere, which it nails in all of its themepark worlds, but a very specific capturing of this certain feel. While visually it leans spooky but still definitely horror, the story and lore paints this very solid 1990s ambient, anxious fear that permeates all aspects of it. Even going through and piecing together the twists (some of which are also heavy handed or pointed at just a little too often I feel), you reach the end of the game without going "I knew it!" but instead thinking ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ it is so sick that they followed through on this, because it owns. It commits to an awesome idea, a blunt fear, the characters are all surprisingly great for such a short runtime, everything about the story and characters is extremely likeable (even if our MC is a little obtuse, it's mostly excusable). They even have a lil himbo horror cop, it's cute. It just knows what's good and does it. The games is too short to give specific details I feel. 
 
Overall, I didn't expect to get as much out of this game as I did. If you're the kind of person who's seen it all when it comes to survival horror and are massively worn out and jaded by the majority of new-age horror games despite how much you still love the genre, I think you will find this game seriously refreshing. it's not perfect, but at a sub 10 hour playtime for all secrets on the hardest difficulty, I think you're gonna walk away feeling like you had almost as much fun playing it as the devs did making it. At the very least, it's not SH2R lol.

comment_evidence.clause: outside of the shared aesthetic this game handles waaaay better than any PS1 title ever did and features none of the janky camera angles (looking at you Resident Evil)
comment_evidence.full_review:
Crow County is a wonderfully succinct and self-contained adventure horror RPG. This game features a stylish PS1 retro aesthetic that really clicked with me - it's sort-of similar to Animal Well insofar as it's a "new" game trying (and succeeding) to look "old". That said, outside of the shared aesthetic this game handles waaaay better than any PS1 title ever did and features none of the janky camera angles (looking at you Resident Evil). Don't underestimate the scares though, this game will get you to jump (at least a few times). 

I beat this game in 8 hours playing very casually and unfocused on collectables which is very uncharacteristic for me. Honestly, I was just so much more engaged in progressing through the story and figured I would be rewarded for doing so (and I was right). I was equally enamored with the puzzles which threaded the needle of "too easy" vs. "too hard" perfectly. I felt like such a lil' braniac solving the puzzles the game presented even if they weren't all that difficult. I only ever got stumped once and, honestly, it was my own fault. 

Tl;dr buy this game - it's high quality and it's on sale until February 24th. The fact this takes under 10 hours to beat means you aren't sinking time into it even if you don't love it, and trust me, there will come a night you're gonna be bored and feel like getting spooked. 

10/10

comment_evidence.clause: I think my favorite part is how the game encourages you to pay close attention--to scrutinize the environment carefully for both traps and resources--which only serves to highlight just how well-executed the art style is
comment_evidence.full_review:
If I had a nickel for every inexplicably-good Resident Evil spiritual successor using a deceptively simple artstyle to hide a well-executed story, I'd have two nickels. One of them has the My Friendly Neighborhood logo on it. The other came from Crow Country. 
 
I think my favorite part is how the game encourages you to pay close attention--to scrutinize the environment carefully for both traps and resources--which only serves to highlight just how well-executed the art style is. It's a love letter to the look and feel of PS1-era survival horror. It's hard to describe just how well it all fits together. 
 
First playthrough took 5 hours (I found all the standard secrets, and had extra lives set to 'on'--I lost two and had three remaining at the end). I'm kicking myself for not [spoiler]reading the note that Mr. Crow gave me[/spoiler], but I unlocked access to a new kind of secret by beating the game the first time, so I kinda wanna do another run. comment_evidence.clause: I wish the studio good luck with future installments however I feel this product should rather be placed as part of a Netflix (or similar) lineup as an animated show that it is instead of misrepresenting it as a "game"
comment_evidence.full_review:
So its very hard to give this a fair rating here because of the way steam works. If there would be a neutral option I would choose that.

I am honestly suprised by all the high ratings here. Not because Dispatch is not a polished and good product but because this is the loosest interpretation of the word game I can think of.

I played and enjoyed games like the Wolf Among Us and this game shares that DNA with an even greater polish on the visual storytelling, amazing voice acting etc. But to charge 30 EUR for what is essentially a nicely animated and voiced Netflix show with the very occasional dialogue choice prompt and 2 very minimalistic mini games and call it a full on game feels just wrong to me.

Was I entertained? Sure. But did I buy a game? No way.

I wish the studio good luck with future installments however I feel this product should rather be placed as part of a Netflix (or similar) lineup as an animated show that it is instead of misrepresenting it as a "game".

comment_evidence.clause: The art direction is lovely and if this was a short little movie on streaming to watch I'd recommend it but alas this is marketed as a GAME and can at best recommend a purchase if you see Dispatch offered on a steep sale
comment_evidence.full_review:
This a glorified game movie, what little "gameplay" that is offered amounts to a few meaningless non choices in dialogue to pick (you dont even need to the game will choose for you if you dont select) and I'm sorry but "quick time events" do not amount to playing this show I am watching. There are no options to skip or fast forward through the tedious cut scenes either. I have seen mobile games ten years ago that were more involved and enjoyable than the dispatch "minigame" presented to the player to navigate through. The art direction is lovely and if this was a short little movie on streaming to watch I'd recommend it but alas this is marketed as a GAME and can at best recommend a purchase if you see Dispatch offered on a steep sale. This "game" is in my opinion, not worth anywhere near the full retail price.

**edit after completing the game** My initial assessment was correct, this is a nice interactive movie to watch. There is no penalty if you dont choose a dialogue option the game will automatically choose for you. Essentially, Dispatch is one long cut scene cut into "chapters" with an optional hacking minigame akin to picking a lock in elderscrolls, and a glorified diceroll simulator masquerading as a loose rts element where you choose hero's to go on calls around the city (again this does not matter success or failure does not affect the story). The qte's I dont even count as gameplay as you can completely turn them off lol. I suppose you can use this "game" to farm some easy achievements but really enjoy it for what it is, Dispatch is a one off season of an animated superhero story so pay what you think THAT experience is worth. Your choices do not matter, your success in minigames do not matter, you just sit back and watch the show.

comment_evidence.full_review:
This is not really a game, but a "visual novel" with mostly meaningless interactions and "choices" and a mediocre minigame ("hacking") that made Paradroid in the 80s look sophisiticated. 

At least that was the impression I got working through the prologue, where I invested 45 minutes (and felt longer) of cutscenes (is it still a cutscene if it's the majority of the content?) which were full of lots of meaningful looks and not really a lot going on. You can't even skip through the filler.

I had about 3 minutes of the aforementioned "game", which just felt like another barrier until something actually happens. I realise there's supposed to be more to this, like managing your team (which I thought the game would be about) but considering the amount of non-gaming content in the prologue I didn't want to risk wading through more exposition, for what was looking more and more to be minimal actual game content.

I'm sure this a great buy for those who like this sort of thing - the positive reviews suggest it has something going for it - but this is absolutely not the sort of thing for me and from what I saw is barely a "game".

comment_evidence.clause: I thought I'd be able to quickly navigate a game I've finished before but nope its really a visual novel/TV series that will make you re-watch the entirety of unless you made strategic save files of planning to replay from specific choices
comment_evidence.full_review:
Dispatch would make a perfectly fine Invincible knockoff TV series but as a game it's eeeehhhh... 

Essentially if you don't attempt to solve every problem with your ♥♥♥♥ or fists the game thinks you're a fence sitter. This is paired with a time-based game play system where half of the context and dialog is interrupted or cut off due to you keeping up with the flow of the game; meaning you need to back out and risk missing out on a mission due to timeout to actually have an understanding as to what your course of action should be. On top of that the early missions are so simple I was able to upgrade most of my characters to be well rounded powerhouses  that can solo jobs. Come later chapters and there are auto mission failures if a hero is too proficient in a specific skill, well guess what EVERYONE on my roster is fully proficient so there was a good number of jobs I would just let time out because my heroes were too damn good at what they needed to do, so by doing it they would just auto fail? Finally the ending... or at least the ending I got, I mostly saw coming making it pretty anticlimactic on top of that its one of those endings where you get to make no post game choices, you just assume that things go on. You do get to make a choice on the future of one villain but they REALLY REALLY try to get you to choose the "awe shucks they learned their lesson" option rather than the sensible one.

TLDR: 100% a game you can just watch a Youtuber play, great art and dialog for the most part but if I knew anyone who was thinking about playing this game I would recommend they play for free on my account.

EDIT: Going back to choose choices I didn't make on my first play through I'm realizing how hard practically every character in this novel/"game" is trying to speak like they're Spider-Man but every third to fifth word has to be a swear rather than a good quip. The thing that sucks the most about that is that THERE IS NO WAY TO SKIP. I thought I'd be able to quickly navigate a game I've finished before but nope its really a visual novel/TV series that will make you re-watch the entirety of unless you made strategic save files of planning to replay from specific choices.

comment_evidence.clause: -Although I prefer playing games with more of a vibrant colorful art style (it gets pretty taxing emotionally to play a rogue lite such as "Darkest Dungeon")
comment_evidence.full_review:
I really love this mash up rogue-like deck builder!  It's a simple concept to mix some of the dynamic elements of "space invaders" but it works really well and is well integrated into many of the card's abilities and enemy behaviours which really make sense.  There's a lot of really creative cards and the overall quality of the game design choices is the strongest element for me for StarVaders!

pros:
-Just played for a few hours but it's clear I was just scratching the surface regarding content!
-Really well designed deck-building rogue lite with lots of interesting cards and solid synergies to plan for.
-You move through the "biomes" pretty rapidly so on a re-run, it felt pretty fresh.  Also events were being modified (such as a new enemy type dropped in a previously passed biome) which mixed it up well!

cons:
-Although I prefer playing games with more of a vibrant colorful art style (it gets pretty taxing emotionally to play a rogue lite such as "Darkest Dungeon"), the art and music isn't really to my taste.  Probably because I'm not necessarily that much of an anime fan.  The quality of the effects are quite decent however!
-I guess the music is inspired from the "arcade" space invaders electronic/dance style?  It's a little over the top for me.  For a turn based strategy game, I would have preferred something more minimalist and contemplative - perhaps just pumping up to the high energy stuff for boss fights.
-Price seems a little high for me for this genre of game, but getting it on sale would be a great deal!

comment_evidence.clause: There's an overwhelming amount of mediocre Visual Novel/E-book style cutscenes in this game
comment_evidence.full_review:
StarVaders is an insanely overpriced and overrated mobile app in exile (at least I didn't see it on any of the app stores, that was a surprise to me).  It's basically Slay the Spire meets Space Invaders.  Plotwise, you control a mech and defeat aliens, but really the plot is kinda thin and bears little relation to the game.

The gameplay itself takes place on a five column grid.  The Space Invaders are of course heading towards the planet at the top of the grid, and you move your robot around and shoot them.  Here's where the Slay the Spire bit comes in... your moves are all cards, and of course you need to get the right card combos to move, shoot the aliens, and then deal with the "additive" spins like aliens with shields and so on... you get the idea.

It's amazing how something can be needlessly convoluted yet exceptionally boring all at the same time.

There's an overwhelming amount of mediocre Visual Novel/E-book style cutscenes in this game.  The developers failed one of the most basic, fundamental requirements of game design.. "Show, don't tell."  So you'll spend a huge amount of time not playing the game, but clicking through endless lines of poorly written VN text cutscenes because the developers couldn't work out how to relate their narrative through the game mechanics, and decided instead it would be better to compete with reading a book for your time.

We're here to play games, not read through hours of garbage intersituals.  Your gaming rig is not a Kindle.

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

While there are options to change the resolution for the game, all this does is scale up the simplistic 2D art assets used to make the game, which makes little or no difference to the graphics quality.  Without any other substantial graphics tweaks, it's not possible for gamers to improve the lacklustre 2D visuals.

The game features simple, cartoony 2D graphics, of the type you normally expect to see in low effort mobile apps.  3D graphics programming does require a degree of skill and competence and unfortunately not all developers have the budget or talent to deliver this, despite 3D graphics cards hitting the mainstream in the 1990's.  Considering this is being evaluated as a PC game, having the graphics phoned in like this isn't going to result in a high quality, visually impressive game that PC gamers are used to seeing.

The controls can't be customised because the game has such a dumbed down, simplified interface that it's just iPhone screen tapping stuff.  The fact that the interface is this dumbed down might be seen as a problem in itself, however... this is a fairly shallow experience if you're the kind of gamer that likes to play games with deep, rich control schemes and interaction.  You'll get none of that here.

This looks and feels like a mobile app, but I wasn't able to find it on the app stores.  Maybe it was removed, maybe it was rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all).

Regardless, for all intents and purposes StarVaders might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities.  It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers.  We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones and play games that might as well be mobile apps.

Those technical flaws drag this game well below the minimum quality standards expected of a modern PC game.

One of the driving elements of this shovelware game is "achievement spam", that is to say the game features a ridiculously large number of trivial/automatically granted achievements, 100 of them, in fact.  It's a damning indictment for this shovelware that people only bought it for easy achievements, and not because it has any serious merit as a real game.

So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 140,000+ games on Steam?

StarVaders has the utterly unrealistic price of $25 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  The quality problems and defects with this game makes the asking price totally unrealistic. It is impossible to recommend this to gamers here on Steam.  Because this is the kind of game you can just play for free on mobile phones, it's impossible to recommend anyone should pay money for the same experience on Steam.

For comparison, the $25 asking price for this game could get you games like "Mount and Blade 2 Bannerlord", "Hogwarts Legacy" or "Day-Z".  Quality, professionally made games like those are frequently on sale cheaper than this.

There are over 140,000 games on Steam, not every one of them is a hidden gem.  I'm here to try help gamers find the ones that actually matter in that sea of Steam Direct self published mess. If you don't agree with my findings in this review, you should definitely buy it, download it, and play it to see for yourself. I'm happy to have helped you make an informed choice, regardless of the outcome.

comment_evidence.clause: The 'more info' screen that shows off keywords and effects makes it really easy to understand what enemies and cards do - that instantly smoothed the learning curve and made it easy to get into
comment_evidence.full_review:
EDIT: I got the 'true ending' in just under 8 hours. I will say StarVaders is on the easy side - I didn't lose any runs and didn't have to grind to unlock better artifacts/cards to win. But honestly, I liked it way more that way, it's fun to unlock stuff and gives casual players potential to grow in power, but still respects your time. The doom system and boss fights are all set up to build that tension while giving you just enough tools to beat them, so it felt like I had several close calls even if I didn't lose. I'm probably going to keep playing too, there's still a bunch of challenge modes and a secret ending to go for. I'm even more confident in recommending StarVaders now! 


FIRST IMPRESSION:
Super sick deckbuilder/tactics game! Very flashy and stylish, very intuitive. The 'more info' screen that shows off keywords and effects makes it really easy to understand what enemies and cards do - that instantly smoothed the learning curve and made it easy to get into. I finished just finished the tutorial run and had a blast, pun somewhat intended. The music bangs too. A lot of people like me saw the potential this game has just by the first run, like the potential depth with the card modifiers and combos with relics.

Definitely recommend, this game has it.

comment_evidence.clause: [spoiler] Moving from the more civilian base to a quasi-cult/secret government base offered a nice new environment [/spoiler] but the story got a bit more confusing and [spoiler] ended on an ambigious note[/spoiler]
comment_evidence.full_review:
ROUTINE! That takes me back. I have been looking forward to this game for like a decade and boy am I happy it was released - and it is pretty good! 

The environment and its details, the stylistic choices and the [b]-VIBES-[/b] are immaculate, as expected. It balances on that 80's/90's retrofuturistic  edge almost perfectly and even dips its toes into 60's and 70's design at a point. Simply stunning work. The CAT is a cool tool and the lack of a game UI made the experience that much more immesive. Some people complained about the lack of a pause button (hitting ESC doesn't pause the game, so enemies could gank you despite you trying to hide behind the settings menu) but I frankly never had a problem with it and it fit pretty well with the rest of the game. 

The game isn't very big or long. It took me around 10 hours to beat and I think the average gamer could complete it in 6-8 hours. The different parts of the lunar base are pretty cramped once you've gotten your bearings and despite the apparent size of the place, it doesn't seem to be able to handle a large quantity of visitors or residents, but that might be intentional - it almost seems like a resort meant for company outings or middle class families.

It is a bit too short - it ends before you know it and you don't get to really utilize the game's mechanics that much, but I can understand why that is given the troubled development and the small size of the team. We could hope for an expansion pack or a sequel.

The horror aspects are pretty good and the anticipation of what could face me around the next corner kept me tense for the majority of the gameplay.

[spoiler] The robots were spooky at first and the environments your faced them in were great, but they were also pretty easy to escape and hide from. [/spoiler]

The second part of the game was sadly not as engaging as the first half. [spoiler] Moving from the more civilian base to a quasi-cult/secret government base offered a nice new environment [/spoiler] but the story got a bit more confusing and [spoiler] ended on an ambigious note[/spoiler]. A replay might refresh my memory of earlier events and close the gaps, but I'm pretty satisfied with the story either way.

[spoiler] As others have said, Entity A is not that unique of a design but what truly spooked me about it was the lead-up; the written logs, the videos, the tape recorders with the moans and gasps and the understanding that this son-of-a-gun was invisible gave me an intense experience before I understood that it hadn't even spawned yet. I had a few good spooks encountering it: turning around after exiting a long corridor to see a tall pale humanoid, only for it to immediately crouch and scurry towards me was the most scary experiecne I've had in a game in quite a while. Unfortuantely, it turned out to be pretty easy to avoid since it cannot bend down and grab you from under one of the many tables you'll find, but the scripted events still got me good. [/spoiler]

The majority of the challenges in the game come from solving different puzzle that mostly follow the same kind of formula; find A, unlock B, go to C, unlock D. It's nothing groundbreaking but it works well enough and with the integrated in-world UI that I mentioned above made it quite interesting and immersive.

At 25 euros, I'd say it is worth it. Despite the short gametime, it offers a very beautiful world and some genuine uncomfortable moments and is all-in-all a good experience for gamers everywhere.

Thank you and Merry Christmas!

comment_evidence.clause: It's like the devs got self conscious that their creature is invisible so they created a model for it which to be fair isn't bad but it's nowhere near as terrifying as when you can't see it
comment_evidence.full_review:
If I could describe it in one way it'd be short and sweet. It's not some 30 hour story game and frankly I can appreciate that. It never overstays it's welcome and it left me feeling I'd gotten my monies worth. If you like atmospheric horror akin to Alien: Isolation or Amnesia then you'll definitely enjoy it too. I've been waiting almost a decade and a half for this game, following their dev blogs for the entire time minus the dark period. Was it worth the wait? Absolutely, that's not to say it's not without it's rough edges as few as they may be.

A few good things before I get into the spoiler heavy gripes:
- The audio is incredibly well engineered.
- The overall aesthetic and environment are very cool.
- It's a game absolutely dripping with atmosphere and dread.
- Doesn't shy away from seriously punishing you for making a bad call.
- The mysterious events on the station are a good driver for the plot that made me want to know more.
- Worldbuilding was pretty solid with plenty of lore and characters to learn about.
- The use of the CAT is rather novel, it is very tactile and a ton of fun to click buttons and eject modules.

SPOILERS:
[spoiler]After the first half of the game you get to a new area and you come to the realization that there are no nasty robots to dodge. Instead there is Entity A which is slowly built up to with audio, text and video logs to increase the tension. One of it's traits is that it can only be seen via your fancy new Interface Module that you happen to just obtain before it makes it's first actual appearance. This is reinforced in some of those media entries. Instead of relying on sight you mostly need to rely on your ears which is made possible by the incredibly good audio engineering that went into the game. You can hear the fleshy footfalls, retching and wailing of Entity A from a good distance away but it can be difficult to pin how far it really is from you without seeing it on the Interface Module. This is where a big disappointment came in, despite the logs all saying that it's invisible unless viewed with the module it will eventually manifest and can be seen with the naked eye. It will randomly cloak and uncloak with no discernable pattern or trigger. It's like the devs got self conscious that their creature is invisible so they created a model for it which to be fair isn't bad but it's nowhere near as terrifying as when you can't see it. The fear of the unknown is engrained in our DNA and the use of incredibly well produced audio allowed you to imagine your own image of what a horrible monstrosity it must really be. I wish they'd stuck to their guns and went that route instead of revealing it so quickly. That being said it was still fun to learn it's  behaviors and sneak around it so from a gameplay perspective it was still good.

The other thing that nagged at me was that the CAT is underutilized. You do use it frequently throughout the game but it's pretty limited in it's ability. The Ultraview has a really cool IR mode which was only necessary to use two or three times and the flashlight seemed tacked onto it to give it some more function. The use of the Interface Module is split between very simplistically opening locked doors and seeing Entity A. This module sees a fair bit of use but I did find that the viewing the entity ability was a bit too short range to be very useful as by the time it comes close enough it's probably already detected you. I would have loved to see more engineering related actions with it. The troubleshooting was barely used and you had to zap some panels with it. Some suggestions would have been a cutting torch to cut open access hatches and some doors. A lockpicking tool using a minigame of sorts to unseal locked doors. Or even a module that detects magnetic fields to fix shorted wiring hidden in the walls and it could double as a way to detect robots short range through objects and some walls. I just would have liked to see the engineering interactions developed a bit further in an ideal world.[/spoiler]

Congratulations to the team for making it through and seeing the project to it's long awaited conclusion. I knew that you had something special from the original trailer back over a decade ago and you really didn't disappoint. I look forward to seeing what y'all come up with next! :)

comment_evidence.clause: many horror games suffer from having poor sound design which effects the overall stealth gameplay due to not knowing where the heck the enemy is but this game does it incredibly well
comment_evidence.full_review:
Cool atmospheric horror game. I do think the price for the game considering the time it takes to complete it is a little egregious but it's still only ~$30 so whatever. 

In particular I really liked the sound design in this game, many horror games suffer from having poor sound design which effects the overall stealth gameplay due to not knowing where the heck the enemy is but this game does it incredibly well. 

I know I complained about the length of the game earlier but I also think it's one of its strengths, it doesn't overstay its welcome. 

If you like Outlast or Still Wakes The Deep then I recommend checking this out.

7/10

comment_evidence.clause: Atmospheric is an Understatement to describe this as you truly feel like you are inside a Mythical Well where Animals Sprung to life and made it their own Home by adapting to the conditions of the environment
comment_evidence.full_review:
An Absolute MASTAHPIECE of a game, holy hell, the fact that this was made by just one person is insane, and its even more insane how this game is only 35MB LIKE HOW WAS THAT POSSIBLE WITH THE DEPTH THIS GAME HAS? The Craziest thing to me was how many layers it had, every time you think you're done, it opens a new layer for you where the game essentially says "You think it's over? Here's something else to munch on".

Animal Well is one of those games that I like to call Puzzlevanias. The structure of a Metroidvania is its core with exploration and curiosity while upgrades are scattered throughout the map for you to find so you can go back and reveal more secrets of this world that you were born into. You solve puzzles to reveal new areas and progress toward your goal while other times you find secrets hidden in the nooks and crannies of every section of the map in this vast wilderness that is Animal Well. You're not a visitor of this place, you are an Inhabitant trying to survive while being on the very bottom of the food chain. The upgrades you get (or rather tools) when exploring are so unique and playful with the whole theme of the game which I feel like its "childlike Wonder" as this game sparks that creative curiosity that only some games tend to nail it correctly. Everything you acquire has a purpose, whether it's the Slinky or the Frisbee all the way to the pencil you scribble the map with, it all has a reason for you at the end when trying to uncover the true meaning of the game. 

For it being Pixel art the Game has a very unique look to it. Neon Pixel Art is the best way I can describe it as it always looks colorful and bright while it contrasts with the vibrant, sometimes dark, yet detailed background. The water Glowing its reflection on the Horizon while Fog Overtakes other sections of the Well. Atmospheric is an Understatement to describe this as you truly feel like you are inside a Mythical Well where Animals Sprung to life and made it their own Home by adapting to the conditions of the environment. The music or rather Lack thereof aids the experience as all you hear is your surroundings. The water droplets falling onto the ground, the noises of your Frisbee or slinky when being used, the inhabitants roaming near you and squeaking from time to time, the waterfall roaring in the distance while you explore, you can feel the vastness of the place to a point where you ask yourself "How deep does this Well really go". Music is only used in very specific situations, almost exclusively to tense up moments of danger when you are confronting some not-so-friendly dwellers or when you are in a 'safe room' to give you a feeling of comfort.

Animal Well is a game that I will not forget and one that I was very Glad to find all its secrets as it rewards players that want to go the extra mile. A game where being Playful is the main Gimmick as the whole world acts like one big playground for you to have fun in (although Scary at times! but that's how growing up feels like.) An Incredibly unique experience that I recommend everyone to play.

comment_evidence.clause: it must be said that the direction taken for the visuals alongside the sublime art style is nothing short of amazing as part of what drew me into the premise of Animal Well has to do with how the world is presented here
comment_evidence.full_review:
Puzzles games tend to not be my forte as a whole, considering that those that have primarily made it a focal point of their gameplay (Snakebird and the Professor Layton games comes to mind as rare exceptions I've played) find it quite the daunting challenge to make the core aspect of their gameplay engaging in such a way that it eases you into the whole experience outside of whether you are already a lover of puzzles or not which, naturally, I find myself rarely taking a fancy to.

And yet it very much has appeared that all that was needed was a little shake-up to the formula as a whole to make it all 'just work'. Such is seen within the creation of Animal Well, a personal and most ambitious project by sole developer Billy Basso, as the inclusion of Metroidvania elements and a sprinkling of platforming whilst still retaining a key focus on solving puzzles as a strong motivation to solve the many secrets hidden within this indie is all that was needed to add a whole new level of intrigue that I'd never have thought possible before with these types of games!

Before I even begin to talk at length about the gameplay and what it entails, it must be said that the direction taken for the visuals alongside the sublime art style is nothing short of amazing as part of what drew me into the premise of Animal Well has to do with how the world is presented here. To elaborate, this labyrinth is filled to the brim, consisting of many species brought vividly to life with Billy's skillful depiction of these vibrant and diverse creatures as he brilliantly portrays them using what I can only describe as a mystical yet ethereal kind of atmosphere that only something expertly animated in 2D could ever accurately portray!

With the obvious high praises sung on the graphics front, the gameplay of Animal Well will see you explore this surreal yet almost tangible world that appears to take place underneath a well of the sorts. Going from the hub that rests upon the starting tutorial area, the player is free to choose whichever path they feel like taking as there are four main biomes that will take up the vast bulk of your playtime throughout the game as these are home to one of four large and prominent animals that each take residence in their respective homes.

The way that Animal Well manages to tackle the critical issue of backtracking in such a way that makes it surprisingly engaging to revisit previously explored rooms is through careful level design that locks paths off in both very obvious but also in some rather subtle ways too. This is accomplished by presenting various challenges that are frequently presented as puzzles for the player to solve, a few of them leaning on one's platforming skills but never to the detriment of casual fun, and making what seems impossible at first click on that light bulb in famous "Eureka!" style by rewarding players who explore further into the labyrinth with various tools to further their progress into new areas previously out of reach, an iconic trait of all Metroidvanias for sure!

Without risking spoilers, some of these tools are fairly obvious in what they are used for and how they can benefit the player. To give a few vague examples, reaching buttons to press that are simply out of the player's reach, reaching new heights that wouldn't be possible with the simple 3 tile-high jump or having an item capable of holding a button down whilst you do something else that requires you to be in a different part of the room altogether, with one in particular offering a lot of functionality if the player knows how to sing the right notes!

These tools, when used alone, aren't too much to write home about and get their respective jobs done just fine. However it is when you start to explore further and hit a 'wall' where the first or second tool you get in their specific location can only get you so far into the biome when the real genius of Billy Basso's game design comes into effect, seeing as many of the later puzzles will require the use of a combination of tools that each interact with the puzzle in their own unique ways in order to solve them.

Considering that one of this indie's biggest strengths is the sheer scale of secrets and other hidden easter 'eggs' that make for a truly fun experience, since you'll come across many things that you would simply not expect to be there. I say this as someone who has beaten the game casually for the first ending purely blind with no prior knowledge of Animal Well, then deciding to look up guides once the optional puzzles for a particular collectable started stepping into more tricky territory as these then become mandatory for the game's second ending and will test your intuition and knowledge of Animal Well to a much higher degree. Though I would encourage the reader to try an earnest shot at getting as much as they reasonably can before resorting to guides, I fault no one for doing so after the second ending with truly cryptic riddles and enigma-like puzzles spanning the entire map!

It is perhaps this excellent combination of a stunning and mesmerizing art style alongside the best parts of a Metroidvania being implemented into a game primarily focused on discovering the hidden lore behind Animal Well via puzzle-solving that makes it possess such an intriguing quality for me unlike many other puzzle-focused games, although understandably anyone who is more inclined towards action titles or any indie that encourages a different kind of thinking and problem solving attitude will not see the appeal in this rare solo-developer gem of a game.

Before I conclude this review, I wish to make a comparison that helps to highlight just how good players of Animal Well will have it compared to similar contemporaries, a key example of this actually being another indie that I played not too long ago in the form of Beep's Escape which has a more arcade-styled game design to match with graphics faithful to the old ZX Spectrum games alongside having a familiar gameplay loop where you collect items and use them to solve 'puzzles' to progress into new areas and the likes.

What makes this differ from that game is just how much further it takes the concept and evolves with it, the tools alone being far more interactive and interesting to use than a simple 'use item' on the right object or situation. Even more so with the vast amount of content on offer and the visuals blowing Beep's Escape's out of the water! The only thing it falters is a vastly higher price point although, considering the serious amount of effort and work that took Billy Basso over 7 years to complete, I am willing to forgive this despite not being a prime candidate for puzzle games myself!

Though if you are still intrigued with the cheaper price and not quite wanting to invest so much money for a game whose concept leaves you uncertain, I will leave this here for anyone who is looking to examine this type of unique gameplay via comparing two similar titles that differ greatly in quality/content and the price points reflecting this so you can make a more informed decision as a result.

https://store.steampowered.com/app/2286990/Beeps_Escape/

Truth be told, it's not often that we see such indies made by a single developer to this scale, Stardew Valley and Cave Story are two such examples that come to mind, and yet Billy Basso truly has outdone himself in all aspects of game development! Though it may not be a beefy RPG that you can sink 100+ hours into nor is it a traditional powerhouse of a open-world game that offers photorealistic graphics and the kind of immersion that triple-A companies can provide, Animal Well still manages to stand on its own two feet, proud and tall as Billy should be after what he has accomplished, and it is one that I can wholeheartedly recommend to both Metroidvania fans who enjoy a good world to explore alongside those who love a good puzzle that blends itself naturally with solid adventure gameplay!

comment_evidence.clause: I sometimes find myself stuck when trying to make unique mechanics or cool pixel art 2d maps- and this game I feel like broadened my horizons a lot and I think I'll be a better dev just for playing through a game like this
comment_evidence.full_review:
This game is hard for me to decide what I want to say about it.  
Being straight up- to my types of tastes, this is easily bar none one of the most beautiful (if not most beautiful) game I have ever played. The graphics are absolutely amazing and makes me jealous as a pixel artist myself. I ADORE the sound design. Everything just feels satisfying and good. And the mechanics are so insanely unique and well thought out. I often see metroidvanias just become hk clones using similar if not identical ability upgrades- and no shade to that if you can find a way to make new unique puzzles with them go off. So I was not expecting at all the unique items you are provided that truly make you consider all of the possible uses and ways to get around. And as for being non linear and a metroidvania- it absolutely PEAKED there. I have never felt so equally confused and curious and free in a game. The map is small enough I don't feel miserable backtracking to see if there are new secrets but still in depth enough to make me want to do that.  
So by all means this is an amazing game for all of that. 
My only gripe is the cost. Not that the cost is too high by technical means as it is a beautiful and amazing game and the dev 100% deserves that price tag for how amazing the game is. Its just I'm usually a  "wait a few years buy it for under 10 bucks" kind of person and this game even after a while doesn't dip below 15 bucks which is usually my upper limit for games (I'm cheap I know). So if I spend more than that, I hope to be getting hundreds of hours and tons of replayability, and although I haven't beaten the game yet I have a sneaking suspicion I've almost beat the main game I'm assuming and even getting all achievements I doubt will crack me an excess number of hours. But I am a speedrunner type person and will likely sink many hours to learn the speedruns.  
I do not regret getting this game (although it was a gift from a family member), and do think it is worth its price, thats the only downside I have (if it wasn't clear the gripe is just the length of the game). 
 
In short: Most beautiful game I've ever played, amazing and satisfying sound design, extremely unique puzzles and mechanics, very enjoyable map and gameplay, and overall I'd recommend this game to anyone I can force to play it. Only gripe is the length for the cost. The length is very satisfying for the game itself just yk can't fault a man for being cheap 
 
I will say for me as game development is a side passion and hobby of mine (and something im doing in university hence why someone bought me this game as a gift- they called it a "school expense"), this game has been VERY inspiring for me. I sometimes find myself stuck when trying to make unique mechanics or cool pixel art 2d maps- and this game I feel like broadened my horizons a lot and I think I'll be a better dev just for playing through a game like this. So if any of yall are devs and think what I said applies to you then yeah play this game its great

comment_evidence.clause: It seems so strange to have us control such a bland character and not even do light storytelling in such an interesting environment
comment_evidence.full_review:
Animal Well is good, not great. It has a lot of good gameplay ideas, and visually it's amazing (once you kill the scanlines, that is), but it fails a bit as a metroidvania in large part because traversal remains tedious throughout the game, rather than getting meaningfully quicker to take the edge off the backtracking. The difficulty of finding many of the secrets and collectibles only exacerbates the frustration caused by the slow traversal and large amounts of backtracking. 

The plot of my enjoyment vs. playtime would look like a roller coaster: weak start, incredible peak, and then a general decline punctuated by moments of delight as the needlessly inefficient backtracking started to take its toll. Given the hype, and given how much I was enjoying it a couple hours in (straight up 10/10), I'm actually a bit disappointed now that I'm done with it.

Unless you are confident it will appeal to you, I wouldn't buy this game just because it has an uncommonly large number of uncommonly well-hidden secrets. I respect the effort that went into creating all of these puzzles, but many are so opaque that you could put in hundreds of mind-numbing hours scouring every inch of the map and you still wouldn't find some without a guide. If you fall in love with this game to the point where you never want to put it down, this of course elevates it by giving you more to do, but the juice is not remotely worth the squeeze for most people,

So, while I enjoyed most of my time with Animal Well, I would recommend buying it on sale. If a game offers hundreds of hours of potential playtime, but that breaks down into 6 hours of fun and hundreds of hours of a repetitive slog through esoteric puzzles, does it really matter that there's more to uncover when your 6 hours are up? Or did you just pay $25 for 6 hours of fun and as many hours of tedium as it takes for you to finally uninstall?

Full list of pros:
* Art style. Many environments are downright beautiful and I love the attention to detail with the animations, particle effects, shadows, and lighting.
* Great sound design. It's pretty minimalist, but I love the sinister, mysterious atmosphere.
* Great puzzle design for the most part.
* I really appreciate that it saves your progress when you die and that it revives you on a nearby ledge if you fall in the water.
* The game has a 33 MB install size and it can run on absolute potato hardware. Loads and quits to menu are borderline instant. Other developers, please take notes!
* I adore the inclusion of the [spoiler]pencil[/spoiler]. Finally, I can be as organized as I want to be in a metroidvania map!
* Tons of attention to detail. For example, [spoiler]fans actually suck nearby bubbles in per Bernoulli's principle, and this can even be used to help you solve a puzzle or two! I loved the concept of being able to fly around by landing on your frisbee too; it was pretty magical to discover secondary abilities like that.[/spoiler]

Full list of cons:
* As alluded to above, traversal is way too slow once the backtracking starts in earnest. The map is not even that big; there are just too few ways to travel quickly and too many parts of the map that are siloed behind tedious puzzles or traversal sections that get very irritating to repeat several times. [spoiler]The game leaves a ton of content for after the credits roll, and the map traversal was unfortunately still such a chore by that point that I dropped the game rather than look for the rest of the collectibles. That's something I rarely do with metroidvanias.[/spoiler]
* [spoiler]There is no story. Moreover, in a well full of recognizable animals, we play an amorphous blob, so I felt no connection to my character. It seems so strange to have us control such a bland character and not even do light storytelling in such an interesting environment.[/spoiler]
* You respawn at 75% health and with no firecrackers even if you saved at 100% health and full firecrackers. This is irritating and serves no apparent purpose.
* The scanlines (if enabled), the pixelization / darkening effect when you take damage, the dark environments, and the fact that your character is not always in the foreground can combine to reduce contrast to unplayable levels at times. In some areas and against some enemies it is far too easy to take damage, lose sight of your character, and immediately take more damage.
* I really didn't like having to constantly switch between several items that all use the same action button. I have a whole controller at my disposal; let me use it!
* Some secrets are borderline impossible to find without a walkthrough, and not just the ones intended for the internet Sherlocks either. For example, [spoiler]how is anyone supposed to figure out which floors the top can break organically? They look nearly identical to normal floors and the top is rarely useful so you'll basically never just happen to be using it in the right place.[/spoiler]
* I got pretty stuck a couple times in this game, even on the main "story", and it killed the pacing by swapping progression for hours of mostly fruitless backtracking. For example, [spoiler]I had no idea what an "M disc" was; even if it hadn't been like a week of real time and 8 hours of game time since I last saw the "mock disc", the different capitalization and the fact that you can't place your frisbee on the M. disc shrine but you can place it in the dog statue's mouth both work counter to any intuition I might have had there. This is especially poor design in a metroidvania, as it's hard to know which puzzles aren't solvable because you're missing the next key item.[/spoiler]
* Lots of irritating little control issues. Menus are hard to navigate accurately with the controller d-pad because even a quick press is treated as if you were holding down a button. You should also be able to use Y to open and close your inventory rather than the close button being different, and you should be able to cancel the flute by hitting RB or LB, as having to hit B is different than how all other items work.
* Jumping from ladders is inconsistent. I never figured out why. Half of the time I just fell off instead.
* The game doesn't pause when you pull up your map, but it does when you open your inventory.
