comment_evidence.full_review:
It's a great metroidvania full of cool and crazy ideas but with severe keyboard accessibility issues, especially on non-US keyboards that swap keys (e.g. German keyboard swaps Y and Z).

Do yourself a favor and get AutoHotkey if you plan to play with keyboard. A .ahk file with the following 4 lines maps the inventory controls from their all-over-the-place locations onto the cursor keys so you can play with WASD+Space for movement plus cursor keys for inventory:

Left::1
Right::3
Up::X
Down::Z

And when the GUI tells you to press "]" it does not work either, but pressing "2" does work.

comment_evidence.clause: - I still love the improvement in graphics and the quality of life features like being able to switch weapons without going into the inventory menu to manually switch it out
comment_evidence.full_review:
My impressions of the game changed a lot throughout my time playing, and CQIII went from being an okay game in the series to my favorite one. 
 
[h1] First impressions: [/h1] 
- better graphics, smooth combat/gameplay, stunning visuals 
- I'm disappointed there're no longer emoticons above characters like there were in CQII 
- map is much smaller, feels more like "small open world of archipelagos" than "vast open seas" 
- loved certain ideas/concepts/gameplay in quests and areas of the map 
- loved the puns (like always) 
- don't like lack of dungeons 
- not a lot to do (much smaller amount of quests, more tasks to complete in each; very few caves/dungeons other than main quests) 
- quests, dungeons, combat, tasks mostly limited to a small number or confined to specific locations 
  - (in previous games, could enter what felt like 20-30 dungeons/trials in a single landmass - lots of options for lower/middle/higher levels - they were more clustered than isolated although they were all spread around the map) 
  - now feels like at most 2 dungeons/caves on 1 island, and less than 10 in the entire map 
- chests almost entirely confined to rewards from completing quests and finding hidden secrets (I like hidden secrets from discoveries; I don't like struggling so much more to find items compared to previous games - I used to just go to the closest dungeon in either location or level difference and just complete them to get rewards) 
- it felt like I had to keep actively searching for more things to do vs just exploring the world and finding things naturally 
 
Overall, my initial impressions were that it was worth the wait, and I had a lot of fun...but it was partially an empty experience. I felt like I was missing (out on) something a lot of the time. 
 
 
[h1] After completing the game: [/h1] 
- CQIII might be my favorite in the series. A lot of the critiques or things I didn't like initially didn't bother me as much after I had completed most of the game. 
- I still love the improvement in graphics and the quality of life features like being able to switch weapons without going into the inventory menu to manually switch it out, and also the manual speed up option for almost all of the dialogue and cutscenes. (This was one of the things I wish had been available in the previous two games, but I'm happy we have it now.) 
- One of the things I still don't like is the removal of emoticons, but I do like the shaky text that comes up when there's an extreme reaction to an event or news so the game doesn't feel completely devoid of emotion. 
- The map being so much smaller doesn't bother me as much anymore since it's much easier to figure out where everything is and to travel all around the map in a short amount of time. (I do wish we had teleport points though.) 
- There were a couple concepts and side quests that made me love this game. One was the [spoiler] 8-bit [/spoiler] castle in the upper left of the map and the other was [spoiler] rewriting the story of the lovers [/spoiler] in the format of a [spoiler] choose-your-own-adventure game [/spoiler]. 
- I still wish we had more dungeons since there would've been more to do, but I think I actually prefer having fewer quests that last longer vs having many short quests. I loved all of the questlines, compared to the previous games where there were a couple I completely hated. 
- I still can't believe that the Gentlebros gave us GUNS but it makes purrfect sense since we're pirates and I love the combat mechanic they have. 
- I loved the other gameplay mechanics implemented for the concept of pirates like being able to steer the ship we stole and shoot cannons and add upgrades to it, and also the bounties, which were more long-term goals to complete alongside the main quest. 
- I don't like how slow it is to move in water, although the plus side is we can go in the water from the start of the game compared to later on in the previous games. 
- (After completing everything: I also miss the [spoiler] Duck of Doom [/spoiler] casually floating by in the background or just appearing out of nowhere and also [spoiler] Aelius [/spoiler] just vibing in the middle of nowhere at the most random times.) 
 
I think I would initially rate CQIII a 7/10 but I would bump it up to 9/10 after completing everything. I still wish there was more content but I'm really happy with what we have. My favorite parts were the changes to combat in terms of having different types of weapons and being able to switch between them, the pirate ship and bounties, and the quests.

comment_evidence.full_review:
A solid entry in the Cat Quest series. It is the shortest of the bunch, and the most minimal, but a solid entry nonetheless. It is pirate themed and has significantly less equipment variety in the series, with most of it fitting this pirate theme. Despite the less content, almost all of the side content blends with the main quest, so it feel very coherent overall. I can't speak for the co-op as I didn't have a co-op buddy for CQIII like I did for CQII.

Pros:
Very coherent
Almost all items are viable
Interesting puzzles
Cat puns
Ties the stories together and sets the path for a fourth game
New ship mechanics are interesting
New perspectives in certain dungeons make for a fresh feeling
More varied boss movesets with phases 
Infinity Tower (their version of the Bloody Palace from DMC4)

Cons:
Fewer weapon and spell variety
Overall fashion feels worse
Very occasional issues with the camera making it so you can't see what is going on
Wizards who are unhitable for way too long in infinity tower

Neutral:
Changed out long-time characters for new ones
The lighting guitar is worse than the lightning axe since it knocks enemies back out of range and you only hit with the much weaker lightning strikes. Neutral because I like the regular axe better but a bummer to see a legendary weapon worse than a normal one.

Overall: Easy recommend if you like previous Cat Quest games or are looking for a co-op game.

comment_evidence.clause: This visual style is a method that lazy devs often use when they have a lack of interest/capability to create highly detailed
comment_evidence.full_review:
Cat Quest III is a handheld (Nintendo Switch)/console game that's also been put on Steam as a bit of an afterthought, as it's very much designed for the handheld/console gaming audience.

It's the third in a series of cat themed RPG-lite Nintendo games with incredibly shallow, simplistic gameplay, basically a very weak 3D shooter/brawler with mild RPG elements.  More style than substance, and with very little in the way of style, the game's success is completely, soley due to the fact it has cartoony looking cats in it. 

There's an overwhelming amount of mediocre Visual Novel/E-book style cutscenes in this game.  The developers failed one of the most basic, fundamental requirements of game design.. "Show, don't tell."  So you'll spend a huge amount of time not playing the game, but clicking through endless lines of poorly written VN text cutscenes because the developers couldn't work out how to relate their narrative through the game mechanics, and decided instead it would be better to compete with reading a book for your time.

We're here to play games, not read through hours of garbage intersituals.  Your gaming rig is not a Kindle.

On the upside, the game does feature customisable controls and resolution, so at least some of the basic, minimum requirements have been met.  Unfortunately there's a number of other technical defects and shortcomings which contribute to the game being difficult to recommend to gamers.

Because this is designed for handheld/portable gaming appliances, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the low power handheld gaming appliances that the game was designed for.  These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the mobile game developers.  The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for low power handhelds forces upon a game.  While this might run well on a Steam Deck, we must remember the vast majority of gamers here are gaming on PC.

The game features low-polygon "retro" assets with cartoony, mobile app style shader effects, making this look like a barely functional mobile app from 15 years ago.  Worse, the developer couldn't work out how to make 3D models of cats so the characters in the game are just 2D textures on flat objects in game (Wolfenstein 3D style). 

This visual style is a method that lazy devs often use when they have a lack of interest/capability to create highly detailed, high poly models and instead use shader effects to disguise that shortcoming under the name of "art", or "We made it look bad on purpose", which really isn't something gamers should have to put up with.  It's unclear why the developers weren't willing to arrange high quality, high polygon count contemporary assets and high resolution textures for the game.  It's far below the state of the art visuals gamers expect as a result of their decisions.

PC gamers will be insulted by the demand from the developer that a console peasant children's toy controller should be used, despite this being on PC.  Developers should try to be aware which platform they're developing for, and must never, under any circumstances dictate to gamers how their games are to be experienced.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 130,000+ games on Steam?

Cat Quest III has the cash grab price of $20 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.

For comparison, the $20 asking price for this game could get you games like "The Outer Wilds", "Yakuza 0" or "Stray".  Quality, professionally made games like those are frequently on sale cheaper than this.

comment_evidence.clause: And personally speaking I appreciate that there isn't an NPC following me everywhere randomly triggering enemy attack animations and resetting attack timers while I'm trying to kite them
comment_evidence.full_review:
People make a lot of comments on the game's brevity but I think it adds to the experience rather than detracts. It's exactly as long as it needs to be without making you feel bogged down by the weight of numbers.

The story especially benefits from this. The entire story, every side-quest even, deals with some level grief or loss. If the game stayed too long in any of the stories they would actually lose their punch. As it stands I absolutely love the small stories in this game and multiple times they made me stop playing and go hug my children. Can't get a much better recommendation than that.

As for gameplay it's a massive improvement to Cat Quest 2. Still room for improvement on the gun balancing (they suck) but the new spells are awesome, the new mana system is basically a more succinct version of CQ2, you get Fast Furward as a toggle once you beat Mew Game with it (huge QoL), and there's generally a lot more room for tackling higher level enemies than the rather binary action in CQ2. The ship feels great to pilot and just zoom around the map. And personally speaking I appreciate that there isn't an NPC following me everywhere randomly triggering enemy attack animations and resetting attack timers while I'm trying to kite them.

Graphically it's a huge improvement as well. There's a lot more dungeon variety, more quest variety, everything just looks and feels better. Music is on point. Map exploration is rewarded meaningfully and is highly encouraged. NG+ is given a lot of slack (on time investment) if you choose to take it. All around just great choices and improvements made by the Bros. Can't wait for CQ4.

comment_evidence.clause: It's not that bad with other large fish on those maps but it's also either almost straight into the boat or up to 1-2 minutes of tedium
comment_evidence.full_review:
Beautiful pixel graphics, mostly nice ambient sounds sometimes interrupted by some music, very casual game play which holds up for the most part. Also doubles as a neat screen saver if you're into the whole idle game aspect. So far, so good... recommended. Until you get into the last set of maps where it can get frustrating. While the river/lake stuff is easy - get fish into boat, sell fish, upgrade gear, maybe take 30-60 seconds for the larger/trophy ones. Fun. Really. 

It's only in the late game where you realize that the reeling in mechanic is nothing more than rolling a die and hoping for the game to give you the win. There's no apparent stamina / exhaustion mechanic, the skill ceiling is so shallow it might as well be the ground. Reeling in the trophy Pacific Halibut took me at least 5 minutes of holding mouse button, waiting for the appropriate signal, let go of the button for .5 seconds, start holding it again... rinse, repeat until you either get it or give up. It's not that bad with other large fish on those maps but it's also either almost straight into the boat or up to 1-2 minutes of tedium. IMHO this needs either some more work under the hood, e.g. add a simple exhaustion mechanic, or at least some rebalancing.

Still a recommendation, everything up to that point was actually enjoyable.

comment_evidence.clause: These activities make successful fishing trips feel more permanent because prized catches can contribute to a visible representation of your accomplishments rather than existing solely as entries in a menu
comment_evidence.full_review:
Cast n Chill takes the familiar idea of virtual fishing and turns it into an exceptionally laid-back experience built around relaxation, collecting, gradual progression, and the simple satisfaction of spending time near the water. Developed and published by Wombat Brawler, it deliberately avoids the intimidating complexity of a hardcore fishing simulator. Instead, it offers accessible mechanics wrapped in attractive pixel art, making it easy to enjoy whether you want to actively chase rare catches or simply keep the game running while doing something else.

The basic progression loop is straightforward but satisfying. You catch fish, earn money from your haul, improve your equipment, and gradually become capable of pursuing more valuable species. Rod and reel upgrades provide tangible goals without burying the experience beneath complicated statistics. This simplicity works particularly well because fishing itself is meant to be peaceful rather than demanding. There is always another upgrade or discovery ahead, yet the game rarely makes progression feel urgent.

Exploration adds considerable variety to the otherwise repetitive nature of fishing. There are 16 locations covering lakes, rivers, and ocean waters, giving players different environments to visit as their journey continues. More than 50 fish can be discovered and recorded in the logbook, creating a satisfying collection element for anyone who enjoys completing virtual catalogs. The 16 legendary fish provide especially desirable targets. These uncommon catches act as significant milestones and give experienced players something more ambitious to pursue after ordinary species become familiar.

One of the most distinctive features is the choice between Active and Passive fishing. Active Mode lets you directly handle casting and reeling, providing the more traditional hands-on approach. Passive Mode shifts the experience toward idle gameplay, allowing fishing to continue while your attention is elsewhere. This makes the game unusually convenient as a secondary-screen companion. You can leave your character fishing while working, browsing, watching something, or completing another task, then return later to see what has been caught. The two modes complement each other instead of forcing the entire game into either an active simulation or an idle format.

Cooperative play adds another appealing dimension. Local shared and split-screen multiplayer lets two players spend time fishing together, while Remote Play Together provides another way to share the experience. The relaxed pace makes cooperative fishing feel natural because neither player needs to maintain intense concentration or coordinate complicated strategies. It can simply become a pleasant digital fishing trip where conversation and companionship are as important as the catches themselves.

Your canine companion contributes additional personality and even helps with spotting fish. It is a relatively small mechanic, but it fits perfectly with the game's cozy atmosphere. That atmosphere is further strengthened by the detailed pixel-art environments. Water, vegetation, changing scenery, cabins, and fishing spots create picturesque locations without requiring realistic graphics. The visual direction has enough personality to make simply watching the fishing activity enjoyable, which becomes particularly important when using Passive Mode.

Progression also extends beyond purchasing better equipment. Players can restore a rundown fishing cabin and transform the surrounding area into a more personal retreat. Fishing from the dock, stocking the pond, and displaying replicas of noteworthy catches provide a sense of ownership that complements the collection system. These activities make successful fishing trips feel more permanent because prized catches can contribute to a visible representation of your accomplishments rather than existing solely as entries in a menu.

Completion-focused players also have plenty to pursue through fish discovery, legendary specimens, equipment improvements, cabin restoration, multiple locations, and Steam achievements. The design remains flexible enough that completing everything is never necessary to appreciate the game. Someone can spend short sessions casually fishing, while another player can dedicate considerable time to filling the logbook and hunting every legendary creature.

The major limitation is that the intentionally uncomplicated design inevitably produces repetition. Players seeking a highly technical fishing simulation with extensive tackle configuration, realistic angling physics, complex environmental systems, or demanding fish behavior may find the mechanics too light. Much of the long-term gameplay still involves variations of casting, catching, selling, upgrading, and collecting. Whether that repetition becomes comforting or monotonous depends heavily on what you expect from a fishing game. Cast n Chill is clearly aimed at players who appreciate cozy progression rather than mechanical intensity.

Steam Deck compatibility is a notable advantage. The game is officially Steam Deck Verified, with its core functionality working through the handheld's controls and its interface remaining usable on the smaller display. Controller prompts and general navigation are appropriately supported, while the game can run using settings suitable for the device. Its viewpoint and methodical pacing also translate naturally to portable play, although demanding visual settings can still make sensible performance adjustments worthwhile for players prioritizing battery life or consistent performance.

Overall, Cast n Chill is an appealing combination of fishing game, cozy collection experience, and idle companion. Its Active and Passive modes are the standout feature, allowing players to decide how much attention they want to give each session. The large fish collection, legendary targets, numerous locations, equipment progression, cabin restoration, cooperative options, and charming presentation provide enough substance to support its intentionally simple fishing mechanics. It will not replace a detailed fishing simulator for enthusiasts seeking realism, but as a peaceful game about catching fish, completing collections, improving a personal retreat, and enjoying quiet scenery, it accomplishes its purpose remarkably well.

Rating: 9/10

comment_evidence.clause: I love the way that these character designs have been updated both to fit their new setting but also just carrying them into an artstyle more polished than the distinctly 2010s indie look of the original
comment_evidence.full_review:
Rift of the Necrodancer is a game that played with my expectations at a few more times than I anticipated. The existence of another Necrodancer game at all was an exciting prospect to me, but the way that it seemed like a far more typical rhythm game at first also caught me pretty off guard, like, it's cool, but not really expected for something like this. A lot of this uncertainty immediately began to fade upon really understanding how Rift of the Necrodancer works however, still taking on an approach that feels as if it's working off the idea of learning enemy patterns and logic rather than usually being as strictly input timing reliant on the games that surround it. Such a core aspect of the challenge in this game stems from understanding the charts to begin with, rather than being able to execute them perfectly, since a lot of this even on hard mode falls into place once you intuitively learn what each enemy icon does.

This fundamental point of difference is where a ton of my appreciation for Rift comes from, the way it recontextualises a rhythm game without really changing anything about what you're actually doing, but still making each moment feel like a bit of a puzzle as you're quickly figuring out what each configuration of enemies will make you press. This makes for a ton of really, really satisfying moments where these seemingly incomprehensible walls end up being very rhythmically fun to play, with some deceptively simple grooves at points being especially noteworthy. Hard mode completely changing these enemy patterns in a way that still makes complete sense is also fun, being somewhat more mechanically intricate but more than anything, just making harder to read charts further reinforces the actual core of this game, ultimately leading to this feeling like the sensibilities of Necrodancer having been perfectly translated into this more conventional rhythm game structure.

The stuff outside of that core gameplay is also wonderful, bringing in a few Rhythm Heaven-esque minigames and some delightful boss fights. These minigames are sorta what I expected the game in general would've been more like, but I'm glad that what we ended up getting was something far more distinctive. That said, these minigames are absolutely wonderful and never fail to put a smile on my face, having a far simpler, sillier artstyle that translates these characters in ways that make them look like those random zoomed out background shots of cartoon characters, just the right amount of off-model. The art in general really stands out to me, I love the way that these character designs have been updated both to fit their new setting but also just carrying them into an artstyle more polished than the distinctly 2010s indie look of the original, lots of fun expressions to be seen here. The boss fights bring back a bit of that arcadier feel as well if you're really desperate for that, being very explicitly about dodge timing in what is essentially a rhythmic Punch Out section, proving once again that the spirit of that series will never die. Overall I'm just deeply charmed by this game, it hones in on some dynamics that immediately draw me in far more than what this style typically does, and it's coupled with a wonderful sense of presentation on every front. I'm glad that a legacy as weird and wonderful as Necrodancer can continue to persist in a variety of completely unique ways.

8/10

comment_evidence.clause: Hitting each enemy type will result in a unique effect and there are modifiers that can be placed on said enemies to further alter effects such as delays/advanced on their time signature
comment_evidence.full_review:
Crypt of the Necrodancer was a fairly unique rythem game in that it played as a puzzle that needed to be solved on beat. The difficulty came from varying enemy types with unique time signatures associated with their patterns stacked on top of the on beat mechanics to force a steady pace of gameplay that the player didn't want to fall behind on.  
 
Rift of the necrodancer completely rehauls the core mechanics while keeping the original concept that the difficulty will come from a combination of problem solving with time limit manifesting in the form of beat.  
 
The main change is that the games UI rather than being a top down dungeon crawler is more like Rockband or Guitar hero at a glance with three buttons instead of five. If you wanted a more traditional rythem game this definitely standardized the formula while capturing the glory of Crypt of the Necrodancer but it keeps the problem solving that came with enemies by transferring the varied types of enemy interactions onto the three lane board. Hitting each enemy type will result in a unique effect and there are modifiers that can be placed on said enemies to further alter effects such as delays/advanced on their time signature.  
 
I can see this game keeping me occupied for quite a while. Some of the achievements also look pretty challenging which is also a bonus for 100%ers. All of this isn't taking into account custom songs or daily challenges which I noticed in the menus. Lots of content.

comment_evidence.full_review:
I don't know if I'm just dead inside or what, but while this game on the surface should be perfect for me, I realized about halfway through my first proper chart that I'd much rather play any of these songs in Stepmania or Eterna or some other 1:1 4key game instead of the weird pseudo-puzzle thing that's going on here.

Like I said, possibly I am just dead inside, because this game looks very well made and the music is fine and the menus are nice and all that. And I theoretically love rhythm games, and I loved the original Necrodancer... but this game isn't doing it for me at all. Possibly the 3 keys is a hard no sell, but the inherent act of having to decipher what is essentially 20 layers of visual challenge instead of just getting a satisfying feeling of synchronization is a complete miss for me. Sorry.

comment_evidence.clause: Another thing that's not nearly as bad but a personal pet peeve is that it often feels like the difficulty comes from poor readability of the charts due to the sprites being so massive that they overlap
comment_evidence.full_review:
See, this is another case of "I wish there was a third option". Giving it a not recommended is too harsh, but giving it a recommended doesn't really apply either.

Cause the game overall is pretty great. But most of the time spent on it was being frustrated by the seemingly broken calibration. I've played dozens of rhythm games. None other has ever had the issue where the timing has constantly been off, no matter how you set it. And what's strangest is that it's seems to vary from song to song.

Another thing that's not nearly as bad but a personal pet peeve is that it often feels like the difficulty comes from poor readability of the charts due to the sprites being so massive that they overlap. And if I'm gonna be super petty, the fact you lose combo when pressing an empty lane by mistake kinda sucks too, especially when the default controls are not in a straight line.

Overwise: Great soundtrack, great visual style, great and unique gameplay and its great to have an easy access to custom content thanks to Workshop (though the "subscription" system it has is still annoying for not letting you delete bad customs directly from the game but it's on valve). The story is.. a nothing burger but better than nothing I guess.

Overlooking the issues it would be somewhere around an 8/10

comment_evidence.clause: there are moments where you will be better listening to the song to know the beat than watching the horrible visual clutter that serve no purpose other than to confuse you
comment_evidence.full_review:
This game is a 3 lane Guitar hero-like rhythm game where the novelty lies in that the notes are obfuscated and disguised as a CotND enemies. Some of them represent simple notes, like the slime that is a quarter note; other enemies are equal to rhythm patterns as the golden armadillo represents a “tresillo”; the last kind of them are just to throw you off like critters that goes 2x speed, or that travel in a diagonal line.

So you could say that this game is a rhythm game that heavily relies in memory and pattern recognition more than it does with expertise in execution.  Essentially is learning music again in another language with a lot of artificial difficulty to confuse you while trying to bring something fresh to this genre of games thats long gone stale.
 
There are 2 other modes: mini games and boss fights. The first is similar to rhythm heaven and the second is like punch out. Tbh they are just there to pad out the story mode and there isnt to much to them, they are interesting gimmicks that help the pacing of the story.

TLDR; This game is totally worth your buck if you like rhythm games, with it’s gameplay that is mixture of rhythm and puzzle. The downside, it heavily pushes its difficulty artificially: there are moments where you will be better listening to the song to know the beat than watching the horrible visual clutter that serve no purpose other than to confuse you. 
Also, this entry doesn’t have to do anything with the previous game except for the characters. So have it in mind.

[b]Video Review[/b]
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jVsIQJU3ZWI


[h2]Not the rhythm game I was expecting[/h2]
It's been a while since we've seen Crypt of the Necrodancer. While the developers turned more into Publishers for a while, I was pretty hyped to get my hands on a new rhythm game, unfortunately... Rift of the Necrodancer is not a rhythm game but rather a puzzler game. I've been around enough. What kind of rhythm games do I personally like? I like games I can jump into, play a few songs, and improve over time. Guitar Hero, OSU, Beat Saber, Synth Riders, Everhood, Rhythm Doctor. I like visual reading, not memorization. 

The problem with this game specifically is that you are forced to learn to train your brain around the multi-layered elements of monsters in every single one of the off-beat half-beat songs. It takes a lot of time, and it's very frustrating because it has visual clarity issues with how the monsters show up against the backdrops, hopping and flashing around throwing off your beat and feeling like a chore, not a place to relax with bullet hell beats. You can turn off these effects, but that lowers the visual quality of the experience, just like Medium difficulty is too slow and tedious while hard is too complicated if you didn't play through Easy and Medium practice modes; you're just memorizing the patterns and following along; at that point, the game is somewhat fun but still the polar opposite of what I was expecting. 

I've given a negative review, not because I hate the game, there is nothing wrong with the game outside of the visuals clarity and of course the annoying elements since it's using a mixture of Up, Down, Left, Right using all (4) and then sometime just (3) making it annoying to follow along. It's something that many people will praise because of Cadence, and it's great soundtrack, but there are glaring issues: people don't review properly, which ends up getting glazed over. 

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
It kept feeling like every new song I was playing was becoming more and more drawn out with the traps, latest elements, monsters, and off-beats that were too much of a chore to learn through practice. Once fully memorized, the songs become fun, but that isn't for me. I mean sure, some people will feel some glaring satisfaction with dealing with red harpies and annoying elements and feel overly accomplished with beating a stage, but that's not for me. 

I would like nothing more than to play on a higher difficulty, but to learn the lower mechanics first and then have everything sped up with so many different things to have to focus on rather than to just turn off my brain and focus on hitting the notes and not missing is what was missing for me.

I've done a ton of Everhood 1%-0.9% No Hit bosses, for example. This is what I like. Basic mechanics, very challenging to play through and learn while being very visual at times and being able to transition that knowledge to the next songs without having to jump over so many hurdles for hours before feeling like you accomplished something. 

Rift of the Necromancer feels like the developers purposely made it in such a way that you're piecing together the patterns and that is about it. The mini-games were much more fun than the actual songs, in my honest opinion because they were not complicated at all, but still fun!

It might be a game for you, but if you're looking for a game you can jump right into and not spend the next 4 hours working your way to understanding each enemy color, pattern and rotation for each song, you're going to just feel like you're working rather than playing a game.

comment_evidence.clause: -how the gourdlets interact with their environment is so cute to watch and worth creating a ton of different types of environments to see how they interact with it
comment_evidence.full_review:
This game is marketed as an cozy IDLE game. Meaning you just pop it up and leave it windowed while you do other things. The being said

PRO: 
-adorable aesthetic, I love that you can pick up the gourds and customize them
-easy to build little hamlets and lots of options for buildings and furniture considering the extremely low price
-how the gourdlets interact with their environment is so cute to watch and worth creating a ton of different types of environments to see how they interact with it
-cute soundtrack, and you can customize each buildings music and ambient sound of which there are a bunch to choose from

CON:
- THE GOURDLET TRAIN.  tdlr in order to unlock more content you have to mature your gourdlets. In order to get more gourdlets you need to summon the gourdlet train. It brings a single gourdlet. My suggestions to fix the train:
   
    1. Make it so that the player can choose if the train comes automatically. It takes the game away from annoying clicker to a truly idle experience.
    2. Don't have the screen force recenter on the train every time it arrives. It pulls you away from whatever you were doing 
  to watch a 10 second animation of the train dropping off a gourd, which gets old fast.

Minus the train deal its a fun little city builder with a cute cozy concept at an amazing price.

comment_evidence.clause: it destroys any hopes the developer had of creating a "retro aesthetic" as their excuse for the lazy pixelart compromise
comment_evidence.full_review:
Gourdlets is more of an interactive screensave than a game.  A somewhat, arguably pointless sandbox where you are given a little plot of land and you can freely drop houses, trees, gardens, furniture and a few other decorations and then watch little "gourds" wander around and interact with stuff (like if you build a dock, the gourds will go fishing).

There's no game loop.  You have unlimited budget, and no goals.  The only thing you can do is arrange the different decorations and then watch the little things going around doing stuff.  While it might seem a bit cute, and even maybe charming, this gets boring real fast.  Like... do you ever just let your monitor go to the screen saver and just sit and watch it?  No?  Then you can see why there's no point in buying this "game". 

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

A choice was made to use obsolete, decades old retro pixel "art" as a substitute for contemporary PC graphics.  It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget or talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is extremely low as a result.

To make matters worse, while lazy, low quality pixel "art" has been used, making the game look bad, many elements of the game aren't done with pixelcrap... which accomplishes a couple of things.  First, it shows the developers perhaps could have done better and they knew it, so that's a major screwup.

Secondly, it destroys any hopes the developer had of creating a "retro aesthetic" as their excuse for the lazy pixelart compromise... It looks completely inauthentic from a retro gaming perspective.  Visually, this is a hamfisted mess, a dogs breakfast of bad visuals, and this kind of laziness and poor quality should never be foisted on gamers.

There's no option to change the resolution and no useful graphics tweaks.  There's no way to ensure this is running at the native resolution of your display.  There's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.

The controls can't be customised because the game has such a dumbed down, simplified interface that it's just iPhone screen tapping stuff.  The fact that the interface is this dumbed down might be seen as a problem in itself, however... this is a fairly shallow experience if you're the kind of gamer that likes to play games with deep, rich control schemes and interaction.  You'll get none of that here.

This looks and feels like a mobile app, but I wasn't able to find it on the app stores.  Maybe it was removed, maybe it was rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all).

Regardless, for all intents and purposes Gourdlets might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities.  It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers.  We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones and play games that might as well be mobile apps.

Those technical flaws drag this game well below the minimum quality standards expected of a modern PC game.

You don't have to take my word about how bad the game is, we can measure the interest in a game by how much people bothered to play it.  Gourdlets has achievements, and they show us a very clear picture that the game absolutely failed to capture any interest from gamers.  The most commonly and easily attained achievement is "", , trivial to achieve, but less than 0 percent of players bothered to get that far before uninstalling the game.  That's a tiny, tiny proportion of gamers who even bothered with this.  Ouch.

So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 140,000+ games on Steam?

Gourdlets has the far too high price of around $5 USD (plus another $3 for the soundtrack, so $8), it's not worth it given the defects and shortcomings with the product, especially considering the sheer number of completely free, much higher quality games on Steam.  Because this is the kind of game you can just play for free on mobile phones, it's impossible to recommend anyone should pay money for the same experience on Steam.

For comparison, the $5 asking price for this game could get you games like "Just Cause 3", "Batman: Arkham Asylumn" or "Bioshock 2 Remastered".  No pixelcrap is worth $5. If developers want to get paid the same kind of money as real game developers who know how to do graphics properly, they need to learn how to do graphics properly.

There are over 140,000 games on Steam, not every one of them is a hidden gem.  I'm here to try help gamers find the ones that actually matter in that sea of Steam Direct self published mess. If you don't agree with my findings in this review, you should definitely buy it, download it, and play it to see for yourself. I'm happy to have helped you make an informed choice, regardless of the outcome.

comment_evidence.clause: The UI and building is terrible after the first 30 minutes
comment_evidence.full_review:
This game is cute and has a fun level editor...

and that's about it. The UI and building is terrible after the first 30 minutes. The rotation can only be done in 90 degrees, so its not only really hard to get a good angle but it's also very disorienting. I also couldn't find any form of grid or other system to make it so I can make objects, such as buildings, symmetrical. 

The kinds of buildings and colors you can use is extremely limited, all the houses are basically the same size and look very similar to one another. There's also a huge lack of good foliage items- there are trees and some crop seeds, but no little flowers and only 1 kind of bush. It also always says you "need more mature Gourdlets" to summon the train that unlocks new items, but the Gourdlets mature very, very slowly. 

There is no goal other than make a pretty island and make the Gourdlets grow up. 

A cute game and its price is fine, so if this is a game you'd like then by all means please enjoy. But I found it to have no purpose or substance, making the initial awe of "aww cute little guy!" and "ooo pretty furniture!" falter extremely fast.

EDIT: If you want a game similar to this but with actual goals, check out Horticular. It's also an indie, zoomed-out, pixelated game with little critters you make a habitat for. (NOT SPONSORED)

comment_evidence.clause: the ability to change the color of an item after placing it and the ability to see all colours for an item in one pane rather than having the same item duplicated in the item menu with two separate color palates
comment_evidence.full_review:
Super cute game! Hopefully there will be some more content coming for it in the (near?) future. While it's fun to build/design towns and parks with the items currently in-game, more items, colours, and path/ground/etc textures would be a huge benefit. For example, building shapes that look more like store fronts/shops, dirt/stone/brick path textures, crates/barrels placeable both indoors and outdoors, more flowers/plants, etc. would all be welcome additions to the game, as would a greater variety of items colors in general (brown!). Additionally, the ability to change the color of an item after placing it and the ability to see all colours for an item in one pane rather than having the same item duplicated in the item menu with two separate color palates. Lastly, the animation for Gourdlets interacting with seating items is a bit odd, it looks like they really just walk through or into the seats for most items, rather than sitting "on" the seat.  Overall very cute and fun game!

Editing to add: the creator has a Discord server for bug reports, game ideas, etc and is definitely planning more features and content updates. The game is lovely and I can't wait to see how it will grow!

comment_evidence.clause: In the Likes section I spoke about the pause menu showing the stats in there but it would be nice if there was a button to show the stats in the mod menu so i dont have to back out and pause the game just to see if it's worth while or not
comment_evidence.full_review:
Likes: The replayability that comes with the many mod combinations and body types, as well as all the super mods that come with this game make this experience something that is hard to master but fun trying.  i like the leaderboard where it shows you what mods you picked in the order that you did and the score you ended up with, gives the ability to be able to sort of plan out a future playthrough, even though it is all random. I could feel like running into people with a leviathan (big long snake) build or go balls to the wall with a sniper build that shoots like a minigun.  
 
The only thing you need is skill and an imagination to what type of run you want it to be. The bosses are super fun, they make the game super challenging and make the end game very harsh. You'll die out of nowhere not sure how it happened or you just pick a mod you didn't think would hinder you so badly but in the end was the cause of it all, but it's all fun at the end of the day.  
 
The amount of times that I would come up woith something fun only for me to tweak it in a future run is vast, the customization and randomness keeps you on your toes as a single upgrade to your body type could mean the difference of just getting a bit further or ending it right there. When you get tot eh later stages of this game it is very nice that it can be paused at a moments notice, you can use this at your advantages sometimes, pause the game to look at your stats to find out if a mod youre choosing will negatively affect you if you choose it. 
 
Dislikes: Sometimes the game gives you things that are unecessary for the build you're going for and some of the mods that it gives you show up multiple times without seeing the common mod you were hoping for, but thats RNG for you, you gotta get lucky with that god run to chase the leaderboards.  
 
Games can run for a very long time, this isnt so much a downside but keep in mind that you might need time to put aside to play this as you get deeper and depper into a god run. In the Likes section I spoke about the pause menu showing the stats in there but it would be nice if there was a button to show the stats in the mod menu so i dont have to back out and pause the game just to see if it's worth while or not, it would be cool if it was there in the mod menu itself

comment_evidence.clause: I bought Nova Drift literal minutes after I first discovered it existed because it seemed like the perfect game—the handling and base mechanics of Asteroids with updated visuals and all of the variance and strategy of a roguelite
comment_evidence.full_review:
As a long-time lover of Atari Asteroids, I bought Nova Drift literal minutes after I first discovered it existed because it seemed like the perfect game—the handling and base mechanics of Asteroids with updated visuals and all of the variance and strategy of a roguelite. It has never disappointed me. The time and effort poured into this game is so apparent in how beautiful it looks and sounds and how fun it is to play. It was wonderful watching it evolve throughout early access because at no point was the game bad, but it kept getting better and more complex and engaging and it's so cool to see where the game is now.

I cannot recommend Nova Drift enough; if anything about the premise appeals to you, give it a shot. It is well worth your money and time.

comment_evidence.clause: but it's not as bad as other games I've played and they usually have some significance - there's not a lot of pass-through particles that make you doge something harmless just to end up getting hit by something that actually does damage
comment_evidence.full_review:
This is a deceptively simple game, at first. One of those things that is easy to jump into, but difficult to master. It's my go-to quick session game. No cut-scenes, no prep missions, no dialog. Just jump into a game, go for as long as you can stay alive and see how high of a score you can rack up; a true classic arcade shooter but with enough bells and whistles to keep it interesting.

The controls work well on keyboard and with a game controller, I prefer the the controller for some of the ability stacks just because feathering the engines and rotation becomes important with some abilities and combinations. 

The game modifiers let you dial in the experience - personally I don't like having a "Final Boss", but "Endless" let's me go for as long of a run as possible. 

It's tempting to fall into a favorite abilities stack, but it's really fun to explore the various combinations. It can be a little frustrating at first trying to figure out what each ability does. There's still a bunch of upgrades that I don't understand their value, but I keep finding abilities I didn't know about that required certain combinations of abilities to unlock. 

The amount of particles can get overwhelming at times, but it's not as bad as other games I've played and they usually have some significance - there's not a lot of pass-through particles that make you doge something harmless just to end up getting hit by something that actually does damage. There's power-ups that you can collect, but there's only a couple of different types, so once you know what to look for, everything else is enemy fire.

My biggest complaint is that this seems like the perfect mobile game, but there's nothing like it on Android. Still waiting!

comment_evidence.clause: The rogue-lite element of the game is comprised of selecting options within a menu once you hit a level up threshhold as opposed to some other rogue-lites that offer items that you pick up or at checkpoints
comment_evidence.full_review:
NOTE: those that suffer epilepsy or are averse to flashing lights should probably avoid this game.

Nova Drift is a somewhat strange game. Having a similar game play style to the old game Asteroids, it takes the concept and adds in a rouge-lite element to mix up the game play loop and create an unique experience each play...is what I would like to say.

Game play in Nova Drift can be divided into two concepts: the actual top down shooter game play, and the rogue-lite element. The top-down shooter game play has you navigating the play area with your ship (equipped with standard HP and a shield that has a passive effect), boosting around as you blast any enemies or environment hazards. You also have the ability to phase across the edges of the screen to escape enemy bullets, though the angle you'll exit from isn't always obvious and your own bullets won't do so without an upgrade. With all that said movement sounds really good but here's where the "Drift" in the title comes in: you don't have free directional movement and must instead utilize your aiming to steer left or right to orientate yourself. while an interesting twist, I find it to be a mixed bag as you will often find yourself needing to point one direction but move another to avoid the onslaught of things approaching you which will probably cause a game over or two. Enemy variety is a bit sparse in my opinion, with something akin to 30 normal mobs (including evolved forms that do the same thing but stronger) and about 10 boss enemies with the whole set randomly being applied per level and the only real change being the raw stats. Some enemies are perfectly fine after you see their pattern or attack and some enemies can one shot you if you so happen you lose track of yourself and stand still for about 2 seconds. Overall the actual game play gets a solid approval, but there are many small issues that can compound if you aren't ready for them. And then there's the rogue-lite part.

The rogue-lite element of the game is comprised of selecting options within a menu once you hit a level up threshhold as opposed to some other rogue-lites that offer items that you pick up or at checkpoints; each of the individual selections reset per run but you can unlock more bonuses to get as you play longer. You start with a weapon modifier selection, then a shield modifier, then a ship modifier, and finally get base modifiers affecting your offenses, defenses, or speed (and other things) plus the option to switch any of the earlier modifiers out with new ones. I think this system is not bad (a lot of the modifiers are hilarious and allow for a variety of builds) but it has two major problems. Firstly because the entire thing is tied to leveling up, you will inevitably start losing gains as you continue to play the game as opposed to having a constant stream in other rogue-lites (like RoR2 which I am using as the comparison point). that in and of itself isn't a major issue until it's combined with the second point which is that there's no real way to "switch" a build once you've started; any ability to swap parts that would better suit a change in ship or weapon is tied to level ups (which you're already probably using to make yourself stronger) meaning you basically use the same thing the whole run and hope it doesn't fail. If nothing else I would like to see some alternate game mode where in buffs are gotten differently to increase variety in a single game instance rather than having to effectively start over with that knowledge and hope you get everything you need. A slightly lower issue problem is also how there's not much reason to mix builds; you will likely always go mostly offensive with some defensive stuff to make sure you don't die, or mainly defensive with barely offensive bonuses and making use of the various defensive-offense buffs. could use more variety amongst the types of offense and defense, even more than it already does.

As for closing notes, the game is visually vibrant, but enemies can share coloration with your ship (and the coloration changes so which enemy does so isn't even consistent) meaning you will occasionally lose where you are and die that way while also occasionally having a lot of things happening on screen at once. Music is...there, mostly; it isn't bad but not particularly stand out either, though I will note it does fit the situation in most cases.

Overall, I think Nova Drift is definitely fun game to binge for a couple days then try a run every few days when you want to unwind. However as a long term playing experience I think it misses its mark and isn't quite worth the asking price unless you either got everything else you want or are really into the game play style (but hey there's also a demo so try it out for yourself).

Final verdict: 6.5/10. I happen to like it, but I'm not overly obsessed over it and I don't think I'd find myself returning *that* frequently to it.

comment_evidence.clause: and menus has satisfying sounds and animations - Every deck and joker feels like it has a purpose (and there are some planned changes and additions for jokers such as Matador in the 1
comment_evidence.full_review:
An insanely satisfying and refreshing game - It's really impressive that almost everything in this game was designed and implemented by the indie creator LocalThunk (other than music and Vagabond joker art + anything else I might have forgotten)

This game has tons of replayability and content - being a roguelike game, every run feels new and refreshing - although you may find yourself returning to certain strategies *ahem* photochad :]

Something about trying to get larger numbers and better synergies with jokers is fulfilling - Every interaction with the cards, buttons, and menus has satisfying sounds and animations - Every deck and joker feels like it has a purpose (and there are some planned changes and additions for jokers such as Matador in the 1.1 update)

Overall I can't recommend this game enough - it is super easy to run on any system and I've heard from many people that it's great on the steam deck - you can play it anywhere online or offline

Best game for $15 in my opinion - I usually wait or recommend to others to buy games during the many steam sales, but if you have the means, support LocalThunk and this amazing game!

comment_evidence.clause: it's surprisingly fun being forced to use jokers with effects you once wrote off as bad because you end up finding a new way to get higher scores completely unplanned
comment_evidence.full_review:
An absolute joy to play. The presentation and aesthetics are fantastic. All fuzzy, pixelated and colorful with a soft glow to it as if you're playing on some gambling machine in a casino. Luckily, it's strictly gambling for scores in a video game, so there's no risk of ruining your financial life with this if you're prone to that sorta thing. In fact, it's a great deal for the price, but it's still a bit addictive all the same. I can't help but get the urge to play more when the thought crosses my mind that I might just get that one special run on the next try. I find myself noticing new tactics and strategies out of necessity all the time when it comes to the "Joker" cards, one of the main parts of the game. it's surprisingly fun being forced to use jokers with effects you once wrote off as bad because you end up finding a new way to get higher scores completely unplanned. 
It's not too hard to pick up and learn, and I say that as someone who's pretty unfamiliar with most card games and poker itself at the time of my writing this. It takes time to get more moves in your arsenal when it comes to card combos, there's definitely some depth there, but don't let that intimidate you.

Also for those interested, it's also on smartphones and it plays very nicely on there too. The gameplay loop is perfect for just picking up and putting down whenever you need to, so it's great if you need something to do when you have downtime. The only gripe I'd have with that version is that you'll be missing quite a bit of the visual charm on a smaller phone screen. It still looks plenty good.

comment_evidence.clause: " It's even worse when you increase the animation speed - you just end up playing and playing because the runs are so quick
comment_evidence.full_review:
This looks like a simple video poker game, but then you realize that there is a lot of puzzley depth to it. As you play, you buy Jokers and other cards that give added benefits like multiplying your score or giving you more money when you cash out (to buy even more Jokers).

You end up going down the rabbit hole of trying to figure out the best card combos to get your points into the millions and billions, and see how many rounds you can go with the deck that you customized over the course of your run.

There are a lot of interesting cards to unlock, as well as new strategies to try as you play. Each individual games is so quick that you get into the addictive gameplay and think, "Oh, I'll just play one more time." It's even worse when you increase the animation speed - you just end up playing and playing because the runs are so quick.

I got this game during the Winter Sale on a discount, but I feel like Balatro is one of the classic rogue-lites that many people would enjoy.

NOTE: I ended up buying this game on my phone as well, so the playtimes on Steam do not show all the time I've spent playing this game. I have drained my phone battery playing it, and I lose track of which game and which unlocks I have on my computer vs. my phone. It's easier to play (and differentiate the cards) on the computer, but the phone port is fun, too. I feel like even at double the cost (buying the phone and computer game) was still money well spent.

comment_evidence.clause: Also the modding community for the game is really unbelievable for how much can be played around with for the game in terms of joker effects/card editions/decks/consumables/boss blinds to name some examples
comment_evidence.full_review: For a gamer that has only ever had experience with poker via Luigi's Picture Poker from NSMBDS, Balatro makes the process of learning to make hands easy by giving an overview of how each hand can be made + the result before confirming.  Course with the rougelike elements it can make certain ones easier or harder to accomplish depending on how things go which while it can be daunting at first, it can be really rewarding when the right combination of jokers/planets/tarots just lines up for you from either a seeded run or leaving it all up to chance.  Decks and Stakes also provide some extra replay value as the former can add unique modifiers to the overall run while the latter improves the challenge.  Also the modding community for the game is really unbelievable for how much can be played around with for the game in terms of joker effects/card editions/decks/consumables/boss blinds to name some examples.  Though I do recommend to at least go through the base game first since some can be overwhelming if you don't understand the core of the game which is really great as a way to pass the time for either a brief moment or long term.

comment_evidence.clause: I’m amazed that a game with nice graphics and a moving character interacting with the environment can be less engaging than a 20-year-old visual novel whose entire gameplay consists entirely of making choices
comment_evidence.full_review:
[h1][i]"It insists upon itself."[/i][/h1]

The overwhelmingly positive reviews made me think this would be the next coming of Christ… oh boy, how wrong I was.

Before I begin, I would like to clarify that I’ve decided, for the time being, to quit this game before finishing. I can’t bear to play it anymore, it’s simply not fun at all.

At first, I was drawn in by the pixelated graphics and the story, which people praised highly, so I went in with big expectations. The game actually delivers those in the first segment. The characters and their interactions are engaging, the social media mechanic is interesting, and choices add some dynamic to the dialogue. It felt solid. But it goes downhill from there.

In the next section, the elements I previously praised start deteriorating. The characters become annoying, the cellphone sections feel like a waste of time, and you realize the choices are superficial with no real impact. Certain elements start overstaying their welcome and the game rapidly starts losing its steam.

Now to the element that made me quit: the gameplay. It’s unbelievably slow and boring. It’s by far the worst thing about the game. You’ll spend hours pressing A, D, and space. When you use your mouse, it’s only to get into a place where you will press A, D, and space once again [i]ad nauseam[/i].

I knew going in gameplay wouldn’t be the game’s strongest suit because it’s story-focused. But that doesn’t excuse making it as boring and slow as possible. If it’s story-focused, why not design the gameplay around that? Offer meaningful choices like many visual novels do. Yet here, choices don’t affect the story.

I’m amazed that a game with nice graphics and a moving character interacting with the environment can be less engaging than a 20-year-old visual novel whose entire gameplay consists entirely of making choices. I could easily spend dozens of hours reading and choosing in [i]Fate/stay night[/i] or [i]Steins;Gate[/i] and love every minute. In contrast, I dread playing this even for a few minutes.

Because the gameplay is painfully slow, the pacing drags too. You get long stretches full of nothing and not even the good kind of nothing found in breathtaking worlds with amazing soundtracks. It’s just nothing or painfully mediocre at best.

Worse, the story itself isn’t even that compelling. It’s just another iteration of popular anime tropes from the past decade, oversaturated and told a million times before, and better.

To me, a game’s worst sins are not using interactivity meaningfully and not respecting the player’s time. This game commits both.

It truly feels like the devs wanted to make an anime based on movies they liked, but couldn’t due to budget so they made a game instead. They just forgot to make an actual game.

Do yourself a favor and watch [i]Your Name[/i] instead. It’s cheaper and actually uses its medium effectively to tell a compelling story.

comment_evidence.clause: The Graphics where pleasing and had meaningful transition from higher contrast  in the beginning of the game to less contrast later in the game (fitting because it becomes more sad and hopeless because of the catastophe)
comment_evidence.full_review:
I recommend to read other negative reviews because there are some that I 100% agree with. But to wrap it up: The pacing is too slow and the game ist stretched unnessesarily long, your "decisions" do not impact the game at all (just a few textlines) so its like watching a very long and slow movie and the quantum physic stuff is a bit lame. I very much enjoyed the first few hours but I feel like you could have made this game perfect with just two well paced acts. So starting in the half of the second act it just gets confusing and the plot feels stuck. Also the game lacks some emotion in my opinion, especially with the whole "reallity breaks" stuff because no normal human would react like they did. I would have loved to see more hugging, crying and just being mentally at the edge. For me it just wasnt staged correctly a lot of the time. You could have gave it more deph with better soundtrack and not just a piano all of the time. Sometimes it feels weird how the tracks just cut off completely with no transition what so ever.

But to name some specific points the game made very good in my opinion: The piano arcs with the piano club were cool and I loved the scene where Nicole and Mark played her piece together. I liked his track for the piano demonstration (Wedding Day from Edvard Grieg). The relationship and dynamic between the trio (mark, cathy and ridel) was nice most of the time. I even found the easter egg in the piano club where the for elise dude and elise had 3 different types of voicelines and one was from the "Bee Movie" with the "ya like jazz?", that was fun to see. The Graphics where pleasing and had meaningful transition from higher contrast  in the beginning of the game to less contrast later in the game (fitting because it becomes more sad and hopeless because of the catastophe). The media-scrolling parts where you check news were cool and luckily they did not repeat them in every loop and made them increasingly shorter. I liked the chatting parts as well and that you had parts where you switched between the chats. I saw some people complaining about the piano game being to hard or not that good. I found it entertaining and cool that you could practice other pieces and it wasnt easy but also not too hard and they implemented an option to make it easier if I saw correctly. The minigames in general were quite challenging sometimes but I liked it.

So I can not say I did not like the game and it had a lot of good parts I realy enjoyed! I decided to give a negative rewiev because of the stuff mentioned but also because I find the "overwhelmingly positive" reviews are just not fitting for this game. I would give this game a "very positive" at max.

I just saw that new chapters (dlc) for this game is announced and I am not sure If I will play it. I definetly think I will inspect it when its out and hope the pacing will be better and that they work on most of the critique mentioned. I was happy to see the game was LGBTQ open so early on in the game although I think there would be more room for that and maybe they will implement more of that in the dlc.

I personally recommend people to look through some of the negative reviews of games they want to buy, because a lot of the time, especially in games rated this good, you will find out if you really want to play it and get a better picture of the true nature of a game. So dont let yourself blind by overwhelmingly positive reviews.

The game has a nice art style and design with the 2d/3d idea however the gameplay is just too basic and easy like it's aimed at little children which is fine if that's who the developers are targeting for their audience, the narrator/npcs constantly interrupting gameplay ruins the flow. The game also just throws the answers to all the puzzles at you even on Adventure mode which is meant to be harder? There should be an option to turn this off or it shouldn't be a thing in adventure mode. 
 
The amount of soft locking due to bugs I've experienced in this game is actually insane making me replay parts of the game which is infuriating especially when I was revisiting chapters to collect things I've missed as there is no auto save (weird design choice) so you essentially have to keep replaying the same chapter over and over in the hopes that you don't run into a bug that soft locks the game. 
 
I would avoid buying this game until at least the bugs have been fixed.

RECOMENDED FOR STEAMDECK - BUT NOT PC.

Edited review. Bought a Steamdeck, tried the game on it, and it functions just fine on it. A bit stuttery at times, but not to the point of breaking.

I'm very glad I can actually play this without it being a chore now! I can actually enjoy the music, visuals, and gameplay! It's GREAT! Still, it kinda sucks that I can't play it on PC, as my monitor has better resolution and display settings than the Steamdeck offers...

All in all, I recomend this game if you have a Steamdeck. If you play on PC I can't with a good conscience do so.

My old review can be seen below, which only applies to playing the game on PC. (A decently powerful gaming PC, might I add.)

[BELOW REGARDS PC ONLY]
If it didn't have such awful optimization, this would probably be one of my favourite games ever. But as it stands, the constant slow-downs (especially in the 3D sections) prevents me from enjoying it.

The worst part? This game - if it actually functioned properly - is EXACTLY what I've been yearning for in a platformer. It's worse than a bad game; it's an excellent game ruined by poor performance.

(Also: how, literally HOW do you make a game that runs WORSE the lower you set the graphics quality to??? It makes no sense!)

Please, please, PLEASE, fix the optimization issues! I can't recommend a broken game, no matter how charming it's artsyle and presentation is!

comment_evidence.clause: I think the out of book levels should built off of the reference of different media/game/animation genre for levels and extend them for more meaningful involvement in helping out of book characters you meet
comment_evidence.full_review:
This game was pretty interesting for an one and done indie game, if I had to score it I would say 7/10. The concept was overall good, a paper mario style children story book with reality breaking 3d links awakening mixed with mario odyssey world kinda. Although I would recommend this game it does seem to cater to children primarily. The only spoken dialogue is from the narrator, everything else requires reading if you care for context and lore. The difficulty and puzzles are child's play and their might be one puzzle that might confuse players if spamming through dialogue and ignore context of the new chapter "spoiler" involves you saving a buried starfish. I think the best moments of the game are the boss fights inside and outside the book and the out of book levels. I enjoyed the reference and usage of different game/animation genres, but they don't do more with that which in my opinion was a miss opportunity. One thing the devs should consider next time are the pc controls, mainly for the UI interface it was sometimes tricky to use the menu options with mouse. I was also discouraged from playing when my save got corrupted and send me back a good chunk back, about 1.5-2 chapters, however this was fixed a long time ago. 
 
 Overall this game wasn't bad by any means, but I felt that it was lacking more substance, which may be due to the length of the game and vision of the devs. I think the out of book levels should built off of the reference of different media/game/animation genre for levels and extend them for more meaningful involvement in helping out of book characters you meet. For example something like "splitfiction" would be interesting. I think cooperative play would benefit this type of game more especially factoring the different genres of games and how they would work. I would like to see this in the next game if they choose to make another like this or a squeal.

comment_evidence.clause: It plenty makes up for a pleasing UI and the most complete audio experience when it comes to music and ambiance - I personally love jazz and am happy to see a solid playlist here compared to how it is absent from other productivity games
comment_evidence.full_review:
The most visually satisfying and pleasing productivity tool I have seen so far, at the cost of less immersion due to its isometric view and 2D pixel art compared to more intimate camera angles and flexibility with 3D.

It plenty makes up for a pleasing UI and the most complete audio experience when it comes to music and ambiance - I personally love jazz and am happy to see a solid playlist here compared to how it is absent from other productivity games.
Talking about UI, the productivity tools are probably the most coherent I have seen them in those games, with subfolders for to-do lists and multiple lists folders being very nice, and the formatting on the memopad while retaining the pixel aesthetic feeling visually pleasing and satisfying to use.

The pixelart is gorgeous and each room is more creative and stunning than the last one. The only thing I would like are essentially more options when it comes to customizing your character, like more eye shapes and more color palette options for clothes and items that is already present in the hair. Being able to rotate our character would be nice too, like on the third room bed, or pivot to the sitting activities at the desk in the first room. Being able to have multiple pets in a room would also be nice since there are already given spots for them.

The multiplayer was definitely my main sell on this, and it functions well with good moderation functions, even as it is in beta currently.

I personally like the more microtransaction model, as it makes the ceiling for friends getting the game very low and helps you precisely cater to which content you want to throw a few bucks on. As we speak, I just got the whole bundle on sale for 20CAD, which feels like a more than appropriate amount for the content of a full producitivty game with tons of options.

The currency goes up very slowly, which I like. I focus on what I do and naturally see that I built up enough currency for some stuff.

comment_evidence.clause: however I think the business model is bad and they should just sell all the normal content together at a higher price if needed and remove all the "DLC" labels from all the menus
comment_evidence.full_review:
Its a cheap and cozy game. It has lots of useful stuff like timers and checklists and the rooms are nice. The adding of custom music is buggy and makes the music too quiet. The DLC is a bit excessive, I can understand adding some music albums after the fact for specific/exclusive artists and having a couple, but there are tons. I think adding character customization as DLC feels like they're removing features from the base game and making them paid.

Overall, the game was worth the discounted price I paid, however I think the business model is bad and they should just sell all the normal content together at a higher price if needed and remove all the "DLC" labels from all the menus. The layering of sounds is nice and the little decoration background part to the game is fun.

Either way though W devs for making such and epic game. I will try again in a few months maybe.

comment_evidence.clause: I would suggest adding more maps as doing the same thing on a single maps does get repetitive from time to time once you know the exact locations of what weapons or objectives you must do in order to accomplish the mission
comment_evidence.full_review:
Very great game, it's like Nature's rule, survival of the fittest. You first start off being the hunted, becoming the hunter while the creature was the hunter and becomes the hunted throughout the middle to end of the match. Love the design choice and narrative of the game and what you must actually do throughout the game to achieve becoming the hunter status. A spaceship survival loot and hunt horror game with beautiful designs, when I first played into a match, it reminds me as if I was playing Dead Space but in 1st person. Really gave me Dead Space Vibes with all the blood and dead bodies you find around the ship and looting dead soldier bodies of their equipment. 

One thing I would suggest they do is add more progression as I've literally unlocked everything that is purchasable in the game within 6 hours of playtime. From there on, you just stack loads and loads of Credits with no use for them anymore (I've met players with Millions of Credits already). Maybe give us an option to allow us to use those Credits to bring carry-ons throughout missions or new tactical equipment to bait, lure or momentarily trap the Specimen hunting us to allow us to escape? But then again, most of these creatures are actually very easy to juke and dodge once you get the hang of it and listen for them very well.

Another is add more difficulty perhaps? I have run matches with a full squad of 4 easily clearing Nightmare difficulty in about 15 minutes and this is with just randoms with no mics on. 

I would suggest adding more maps as doing the same thing on a single maps does get repetitive from time to time once you know the exact locations of what weapons or objectives you must do in order to accomplish the mission. Maybe the developers will add new maps of a different space ship or a space station or a facility location on a planet to do our contract missions on. 

Overall, I see a good potential for this game as early access. Lets see what the developers will cook up more in their next upcoming updates.

comment_evidence.full_review:
I finished Species Unknown after 30 hours, and overall I really enjoyed it. The atmosphere, exploration, and discovering new alien species kept the game engaging from start to finish.

My biggest issue was the endgame. To finish the game, you need to [spoiler]collect four research samples, kill four of each enemy, and capture one.[/spoiler] Unfortunately, the same Aliens kept spawning repeatedly near the end, making completion more tedious than challenging.

The unskippable docking and takeoff animations also become repetitive after many missions and unnecessarily extend the playtime --->[i] le me calculate that the start of the ship and its arrival on the map takes 78s, the mission and return to the hangar (the animation of entering the hyperspace along with the hangar) takes 42s the average mission takes 11 minutes[/i][u] soo 18% ( form me prob 15/12% -> 4h) of my playtime are ship animations )[/u]

It would be cool to have Steam achievements, custom mode (selecting modifiers/aliens) and an additional Difficulty 5. A true hardcore mode with no respawn capsules, occasional two-enemy encounters, and limited health and ammo refills would add a lot of replayability. Despite these flaws, Species is a fun and enjoyable game with a unique atmosphere. I definitely recommend it, and I'm looking forward to seeing how it develops in future updates. 

[h1]9.5/10[/h1]
