comment_evidence.clause: the amount of textures and screentones and unique little brush patterns that make up the greenery and towns and city alleys makes it *agonising* how little you get to explore (well except for the sewers
comment_evidence.full_review:
I know you're not boring. 

As messy and convoluted as trying to context switch between the two different track modes during the cop fights, but christ, are there some CINEMA moments. The art direction is stunning, the amount of textures and screentones and unique little brush patterns that make up the greenery and towns and city alleys makes it *agonising* how little you get to explore (well except for the sewers, I could give or take that). Music is, well, I have to laugh how many good tracks they cram in here. Even the ones that are frustrating to map to a rhythm game, you can at least forget that they're keeping score, and enjoy the music. What else do you need? You have something pretty to look at, and something cool to listen to? 

It's basically impossible to keep track of what's happening. Who is doing what, why are they there, what is Beat doing, why? And at some points, you're throwing your hands up while Clef is shouting at you, and at other points, you're breathing a bit faster because you know you ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up, and there's no way the story is going to let you forget it or even let you catch your breath. I know if you're gonna tow the line to strike a balance there with the story, it's gonna be 50/50 sometimes. But you can't fault ambition, and when I played this, I didn't see anything else. 

As little time I got to spend with all of them, it was still hanging out with the twins and Quaver, though I know those days can't last forever. The story seems so eager to give me more of Team Rocket, sorry, I mean Poco/Apoco, and their role as media tyrants, but I can't tell them to make more game. I'm sure they want to as well. 

It is remarkable how many times the game manages to frustrate me by showing me something I wish I had more of or tweaked slightly, and then force my hands off the controller and think "ABSOLUTE CINEMA" the next minute. 

This is the type of game that makes me think that these guys are never going to make another game. It's a one and done sort of thing. No sophomore album. And it might be enough to cement their legacy with a strong enough cult following. 

Someone please get in touch with Julian Casablancas and get a Reptilia chart pls.

comment_evidence.clause: It's hard to tell sometimes if the UI/dialogue system is just clunky or if it's clunky in a way that's trying to express how awkward the conversation is
comment_evidence.full_review:
I am glad that this game exists
I am glad that I got to experience it
My feelings towards other parts are...complicated

The best way that I can describe UNBEATABLE is..."scrappy". You can feel that there's so much passion and love put into it, and it comes out raw and genuine in a way that you really don't get to see often. It's being shown something that has some rough edges but neither of you care because you're just overjoyed that you got to see an idea like this move from thought to reality in the first place.

But........

Those rough edges sometimes need to be sanded down. It's hard to tell sometimes if the UI/dialogue system is just clunky or if it's clunky in a way that's trying to express how awkward the conversation is. This is also technically a rhythm game, but I think about <30% of my playtime was actually rhythm bits (although I love the baseball parts, I wish I could replay those easier).

The amount of love, care, and passion put into this deserves the $30 price tag. But you, the person reading this review, might not get $30 worth of entertainment from this game. unbeatable is messy the way that life is messy, and if you need a little bit less of that, that's ok.

comment_evidence.clause: This game is supposed to be a rhythm game but after playing for 2 I feel like I am using visual cues instead of the actual music to do my inputs and thats with all the camera flipping and rumble effects happening at the same time
comment_evidence.full_review:
Game has a lot of style and could be soo good...
That being said I bought and played when it first launched and it had a lot of problems. The game was unoptimized, the story made little sense, and the "rhythm" parts felt dry. After they started fixing things and the game can now run without crashing but the main issue still remains.
This game is supposed to be a rhythm game but after playing for 2 I feel like I am using visual cues instead of the actual music to do my inputs and thats with all the camera flipping and rumble effects happening at the same time. 
When playing the arcade mode I fell I am just randomly pressing buttons and getting 80% score on hard and expert. I dont feel like my inputs matter to the song playing in the background the reward you get for getting a prefect input is a stale slap noise that doesnt feel like it belongs with the song being played... I mean that is a pretty important part of a rhythm game if it werent for that id just play a beat em up game. 
I also purchased the DLC when the game came out and all of the tracks in arcade mode dont feel like they were made with the game in that your stale slapping noise feels like an afterthought and not incorporated into these dlc tracks. I feel like changing the slap noise into a noise that fits with the song would be a better option but that isnt the case.
I really wanted this game to do well but with the announcement of DLC being announced I feel like it needs more polish on just the base game before going into DLC territory.

comment_evidence.clause: The graphics are not only gorgeous but also play a big role in the storytelling with beautiful visuals that enhance the game’s magical vibe and showcase stunning visuals that enhance the game’s atmosphere
comment_evidence.full_review:
I’ve played Gris before, and I really loved almost everything about Neva. The gameplay is outstanding, showcasing a meticulously crafted design that strikes a perfect balance between combat and puzzles. Each chapter introduces unique challenges, seamlessly transitioning between tougher segments and easier ones. Also this thoughtful gameplay kept me fully engaged while I played.

One of my favorite parts was the battling alongside the little wolf, Neva. The way Alba and Neva interact adds a lovely atmosphere to the gameplay. I love those cutscenes where she hugs Neva, they give me this warm, nostalgic feeling that reminds me of hugging my cat. Neva not only helped me in battles but also added a lot of emotional depth to the story. After each exploration, I also noticed that Neva sometimes took the lead while sometimes she fell behind but I found the joy in calling her name to bring her closer, and taking a moment to give her a little pat felt great—like thanking and comforting a dear friend. I think that this small yet meaningful gesture deepened my connection with Neva, making our journey feel like a shared adventure filled with companionship.

The story unfolds as we travel with Neva through a beautifully crafted world that experiences the changing of four distinct seasons while dealing with shadows of darkness. The plot is intricately woven, filled with both heartbreaking and heartwarming moments that resonate on a personal level. Each chapter contributes to a storyline and leads us into an exploration of loss, growth, and resilience that adds profound depth to the overall experience. The struggles and triumphs faced by the characters felt deeply relatable, making each chapter not just a part of a game but a significant and impactful narrative journey.

Visually, Neva is stunning. The graphics are not only gorgeous but also play a big role in the storytelling with beautiful visuals that enhance the game’s magical vibe and showcase stunning visuals that enhance the game’s atmosphere. Each chapter bursts with meticulous attention to color, texture, and detail, The art style is enchanting, and I love the stylized direction and the scenes that are not just aesthetically pleasing but also emotionally moving. The artistic quality of the game serves as a vital characteristic, enriching both its narrative and gameplay remarkably.

The music is another big part of what makes this game awesome. The soundtrack is beautifully crafted and matches the mood perfectly, boosting the atmosphere of the game. The melodies connect so well with the themes, bringing each scene to life and pulling me deeper into the story, whether I was exploring or in the middle of an intense battle.

It’s clear that the developers and artists put their hearts into making Neva. Their passion, creativity, and meticulous attention to detail shine through in every aspect of this game, crafting a truly memorable experience.

Overall, I really recommend this game. It is a game that deserves to be played and cherished by anyone who loves immersive storytelling and beautiful artistry.

comment_evidence.clause: is that it does a very poor job of informing the player on how they should be contextualizing its environments and atmosphere until the very end of the game
comment_evidence.full_review:
as someone who didn't like GRIS, Nomada Studio's previous game, i was pleasantly surprised by how much I ended up liking this game. 

my main issue with GRIS, other than the gameplay being awfully repetitive and uninspired, is that it does a very poor job of informing the player on how they should be contextualizing its environments and atmosphere until the very end of the game. that is to say, if you go into GRIS fully blind like i did, you likely won't realize that the game is supposed to represent the loss of a family member until the very end because every direct allegory to loss is made far too open-ended and vague. i'm fine with esoteric forms of storytelling, but when there's no concrete idea to connect the esoteric storytelling to like in GRIS, it's impossible to muster any attachment to the story because for the majority of the game, it all seems like a jumble of unrelated story beats meshed together with no meaning. 

Neva still focuses on environmental storytelling as much as GRIS (if not more), but fixes GRIS' primary issue with this over-secretiveness by immediately giving you context on the dilemma Neva and the MC find themselves in. it doesn't handhold you through the plot and still trusts the player to gather the majority of the story beats through its show-not-tell storytelling, but it gets you initially attached enough to WANT to find out more. the game is less abstract and bizarre, which makes the more emotional moments more direct and grounded. Neva's story certainly isn't the best story out there and definitely does falls into some predictable cliches at times, but it was a huge upgrade to say the least.

aside from the story, the art in this game is consistently stunning. the gameplay is also much less repetitive than GRIS. there's a ton of unique platforming mechanics that are utilized effectively but never overstay their welcome. combat isn't complicated or anything but it gets the job done and never devolves into a mindless hack-and-slash. you will need to actively pay attention to the timing of enemy attacks in order to dodge them during fights. there are also escape sequences that felt very reminiscent of Ori and the Blind Forest, albeit lacking the same level of urgency that Ori's escape sequences are known for. this isn't a difficult game, but there are definitely encounters in this game that will have you dying. people less experienced with gaming who were looking for a more art-focused and mechanically undemanding experience like GRIS might find some frustration with Neva because of this.

definitely don't buy this at full price. the main game took merely 3 hours to complete with the DLC taking an additional 50 minutes, and this was with collecting over half of the side collectibles across both.

comment_evidence.clause: The thing that saved it for me was the music and art style of the arena's that sold it to me so the repetitive fights didn't become a problem
comment_evidence.full_review:
TLDR: 9/10
Pros:
-Good and Innovative platforming
-Movement is nice
-combat is simple
-looks amazing
-music is amazing
-keeps things interesting through out the game
Cons:
-Bosses feel a bit too easy (could be because I play a lot Metroidvania games)
-monsters feel a bit repetitive, they do change but are mostly the same repetitive.

Full Review:
-Story 9/10: As someone who likes to get thrown into a world blindly and just explore it and learn as we go, this game is amazing. Not only does the game makes you ask questions about the world throughout the game, it never really gives you the answers, which might annoy some people, but I love it. The main story plays in the background most of the times and then confronts you with it in big moments which is good. I like how the platforming is the main core of this game, but the story does indeed become a heart throb in certain places. 

-Music/Sound design 9/10: As someone who loves classical style music, this game does an amazing job with its soundtrack. They are both impactful and elevates certain scenes to the next level. I would dare to compare it something like Clair Obscure: Expedition 33. Of course not to par with it but in the impact fullness that the music had in scenes and in its beauty. 

-Art style 10/10: I think is one of the best artistic games I have played. Although I would say it looks a bit similar to game Planet of Lana (another indie game) in the artistic design style, but this game is has a more simplistic approach which fits it in an amazing way. The monster designs, although I wouldn't say are unique, since you can see some potential inspiration from The Witcher, Berserk, Fromsoft games and others. However, the way they tie it into the underlying story makes there designs that much cooler and adds unique depth to them. 

-Level Design 10/10: Compared to other games, it isn't THE best in the way some areas are made. Some feel a bit more length in others. However, I do think that it was on purpose. The whole feeling I got from this game was to learn to slow down and enjoy some moments; either the level design itself or the overall view. It takes the collectables as optional but  they are mostly blocked by some hard platforming. I wont say I got all of them because there were some that were hard, but most of them are just really fun to get to and figure it out. If one are used to games like Hollow Knight or Ori, then this game's platforming isn't hard but just fun and smooth. There are some amazing sections where I was surprised by the level design. I wont give spoilers of what and when since going blind in that sense is part of the experience. over all I had a great time with the the adaptability of the world

Monster/Combat Design 7/10- As mentioned in the Art section, it isn't something mind blowing: they are relatively simple however some boss designs are really surprising. The combat is fluid however really simple, even halfway in the game were new mechanics are introduced with Neva, it is still simple, which isn't bad at all. However, I will say that sometimes, during some (mini)bosses, there isn't enough feedback to the player to know that if you are doing the right thing or if you are even doing damage. The biggest example of this could be seen with the final boss in the DLC where it felt I wasn't even doing the right thing until it finally went into the next stage and made me realized "oh okay so we are doing damage". There are some examples of this in the main game, but it isn't everywhere. Now another thing I would say that the combat through almost every level does become really repetitive. Since the combat design is really simple there isn't a lot of room for crazy things to happen. Combos are short and sometimes can feel underwhelming. With that being said once you really understand the mechanics, which doesn't take long (for me at least it wasn't) the game really became simple, which included boss fights. The thing that saved it for me was the music and art style of the arena's that sold it to me so the repetitive fights didn't become a problem.

Conclusion:
Overall, it is a great game, and a game worth playing. I would say that $20 could be a stretch, but for the art style and music and level design I would get it for that alone. It made me fall in love with its' characters and made me love the world around it that is full with mystery. Great game I would recommend. Overall score: 9/10.

comment_evidence.full_review:
i think that i expected too much, but tldr this game is on par at best with GRIS with all same positives and negatives. more details:
- still good soundtrack by Berlinist - in some cases its better integrated in game in non distracted manner, but i couldn't remember a single tune or track after finishin game
- still good visual, but i probably would prefer more contrast GRIS style, somehow there are some places in this game where you couldn't understand if you able to stay on something or not
- still combat sucks - its very basic, limited and just not feeling right, so for players who aren't hardcore some segments could be too hard, but for more skilled players there aren't enough visual/audio feedback about enemy attacks to react in time (for non basic enemies ofc) and no feedback about hits and when you could use non basic attacks
- still there are a lot of places where you could lost and misunderstood author intention and while thinking about looking for collectibles, somehow find yourself on main road and won't able to return without restarting chapter
- still confusing story, don't get me wrong its fine, but... confusing
Update:
- i forgot to mention that there aren't much settings in game except for sound, it runs fine even on steam deck, but you can't even remap controls. game could be better if there will be hdr support, because visual part of game is one of most prominent pros of game

so... if you want something like "story"-focused game with minimalistic puzzles, good soundtrack and wouldn't mind to spend not so big money, its safe choice - buy it, but if you expect something a just little bit more, you could be dissapointed like me

comment_evidence.clause: the way characters and enemies are carefully animated in multiple directions makes a huge difference in making the game feel immersive and the soundtrack + voice acting is a perfect cherry on top of it
comment_evidence.full_review:
I have played barely any "survivors" clones, but I really fell in love with Halls of Torment. 
The most striking thing about it is the presentation; anyone who has played the original Diablo feels immediately at home which isn't a small feat to accomplish; the way characters and enemies are carefully animated in multiple directions makes a huge difference in making the game feel immersive and the soundtrack + voice acting is a perfect cherry on top of it.  
The gameplay doesn't pale in comparison, either; each character having their own unique main weapon makes all of them attractive to pick. The abilities (weapons) have a good amount of variety and the multiple levelup / "evolution" choices gives a lot of room to play around. The equipment system works great as well, being part of the non-perishable progress as well as improving synergies with characters/abilities. The quest system is also made very well, there's a good balance between rewards unlocking on their own and having objectives that require playing the game differently than usual (for example, not moving from starting position or not doing any damage). 
Outside the gameplay itself, there isn't much to complain about; UI works, there are enough options for controls, and the only bug I encounter is the game displaying and icon for item magnets that don't exist (definitely annoying).  
 
Overall, a great game with lots of content and replayability, definitely one of the best in its genre.

comment_evidence.full_review: This game is pretty good. Although it mostly feels like a Vampire Survivors clone, the style of the art is nice and reminds me a bit of the classic arcade / 8-bit game Gauntlet and there is less of a 'ridiculous overpowered' element after 10-15 minutes to this, than you see in VS. The bosses are much better, with a variety of attacks to dodge, though, I feel those could be made harder. I feel it's a bit too similar to VS still. It needs a little something extra; gates with keys to different areas that alter the dynamics somehow? Something that triggers insane waves of enemies? Choices, dilemmas, ...? Ideally there should be something more than just flow-state taking down waves of skeletons etc.  Perhaps stories to be unlocked; random characters needing help being overwhelmed themselves...? Invading other people's games to help them / hurt them? I don't know.

comment_evidence.clause: Then the pacing starts to seriously hurt when you have to check every little square on every little tab of the clunky quest menu to find what specific dumb objective you're going to spend your next run to complete
comment_evidence.full_review:
Vibes are immaculate here, that 1999 Diablo style aesthetic is so pristine this game somehow looks more like the first Diablo games than the first Diablo games themselves. Beneath that is a very competently designed and crafted game. Of all the garlic-likes I've played, this definitely requires the most thought and careful moment-to-moment decision making, which isn't always to its benefit. A couple bad choices will easily brick your run and if you're not absolutely dumpstering the entire screen with infinite DPS, it is very easy to slowly get outscaled.

Most of the time, gameplay is a careful dance around enemies while balancing your DPS and defenses. It's much slower and more methodical than other mindless zoom-zoom style games in the genre, but it's never a slog. It stays engaging and sometimes tense even when you're at your strongest. This isn't the kind of game where the last 15 or 10 minutes are a formality when you KNOW the run is solved, won, cooked, packaged and stamped but you have to sit there and wait for the timer to tick.

I say "most" of the time because the rest of it you'll be staring at quest menus and upgrade screens. See below.

There are two big problems with the game. The first is visibility. It sucks ass just like in every other game in this genre, but it's especially bad here because gameplay is very punishing and some characters can be seriously glass-cannony. Skimp on HP regen and get unlucky with heal drops and every HP you lose can easily stay lost 10 or 15+ minutes later into the run. Some builds and maps are much worse than others. I've never felt outright cheated by this since I like to build a minimum of defenses but it will hurt if your ego is so fragile you'd rather die than stop pretending the answer to everything is "just dodge everything perfectly 100% of the time bro". You can't and you won't.

The second and IMO larger problem is the quest design. As you progress, more and more things are locked behind "quests" which are largely extremely annoying limitations imposed on you that don't mesh well with the core gameplay. There's way too many quests that require you to actually remove permanent upgrades (like HP) and then avoid a specific stat, on EVERY LEVEL UP, throughout the entire run. Others require you to not move or avoid getting hit for X amount of time, and failing that even by accident means you've just wasted 10 minutes of your life and it's time to reset. Others are annoyingly specific objectives to accomplish that likely require a dedicated setup and specific method you're probably not gonna figure out without a ton of trial and error.

Even the least offensive quests often require you to pick a specific ability, level it in a specific way, and then get lucky with it, or reroll endlessly until you achieve pointless ♥♥♥♥ like making the Clay Golem roll for 15 minutes in a run (at which point you're gimped because my poor golem boy is terrible). Some of these would be fine, but there are just so many that you won't play especially long before playing normally just isn't completing any quests at all. Then the pacing starts to seriously hurt when you have to check every little square on every little tab of the clunky quest menu to find what specific dumb objective you're going to spend your next run to complete. Then you have to pick the right character. Then sort through all your items and pick the ones you want for this one specific thing. Then fail 20 minutes in because your approach was wrong and are you having fun yet?

To be clear, there is a lot of meat on these bones that you can chew through by playing like a sane person. You're always progressing towards a few things, even if slowly, and I'm sure some people will enjoy the more bespoke objective-oriented challenges. Personally, I just think they get in the way and have you staring at menus and doing boring busywork planning upgrade routes far too long while I'd rather just be smashing skeletons and burning demons alive. Sacrificing your amulet slot to locate herbs around stages and doing the minipuzzle to nerf the end bosses are plenty if you ask me. I think quests should follow that general philosophy rather than "Deal 2,000,000 lasagna type damage on the popsicle type character without leveling up your attack speed, moving to the right, or talking to your sister for the first 18 minutes and 27 seconds" type nonsense.

If you want a comparably grindy, much more streamlined alternative with a 10/10 soundtrack try Soulstone first. If you played VS and felt the lack of challenge but liked the general type of gameplay, get this first instead.

comment_evidence.clause: I think the combination of barely being able to stay alive - the enemies move just fast enough and I have enough difficulty getting kills at a certain point - combined with better than awful graphics
comment_evidence.full_review:
This game's name is not pronounced "Halls of Torment."  You have to use a gravelly voice like you're choking on something "Khhhhkhkhkalls of Tkkkhhhorment".  At least that's how I try to pronounce it.

This is juicy.  I enjoy it most when I'm exercising and using a controller, as I completely forget about time and how long I've been working out!

There are several "bullet hell" offerings out there ranging from "can't stop playing" to "mildly interesting".  I'd put this one deeply in the earlier category.  For example, compared to Vampire Survivors, this feels much more intense even while I'm still in the early game (and I love Vampire Survivors too).

What makes it work?  I think the combination of barely being able to stay alive - the enemies move just fast enough and I have enough difficulty getting kills at a certain point - combined with better than awful graphics, which lends to some immersion, makes this game sticky.

It doesn't have any voice acting, nor a story.  But what it does have it makes the most of, which is a good progression and a feeling of dancing my way around the floor trying to stay alive while dealing with all the baddies swarming in to kill me.

The game works both with keyboard/mouse or with a controller - wonderful!

And the game is dirt cheap.  I bought it at a 20% discount, but it was already under $4 so who cares?  It's already more than made up for the price.

comment_evidence.clause: The combination of old school Diablo aesthetics and the horde destroying gameplay of bullet heavens is a very effective match and results in something that feels both nostalgic and new at the same time
comment_evidence.full_review:
A very fun and addictive addition to the Vampire Surviors-like genre. The combination of old school Diablo aesthetics and the horde destroying gameplay of bullet heavens is a very effective match and results in something that feels both nostalgic and new at the same time. Halls of Torment switches things up with the addition of gear, a pretty sophisticated system for leveling up that has many possibilities for synergies, and the ability to set your character up with a load out before each run. This extra layer of complexity is certainly welcome and encourages a lot of replayability as you test and run different builds for characters. 

While I have only scratched the surface, I am already hooked and looking forward to playing more. Highly recommended, especially for fans of the genre.

comment_evidence.full_review:
First few minutes of the game and so far I think the concept is highly interesting and have so much potential since it is already amazing as an RPG and because of how it is structured I think it'd be possible to have community-made content.

I found the translation to still be kind of so-so and I don't really think the text size in English fit in some UI though it's readable to me (but I'm someone who have read a lot of MTL media so I might just be numb to it).

The problem I think I had starting the game is that it had unpolished work on the controls and the UI, I wish they address this in the future updates so that the UI can be as appealing as their sprite work which is really really good, 

this also includes how there is controller support but it becomes pretty clunky that it became tedious to me on the controller (I am using an F310 Logitech Controller with Xinput)

tl;dr Great RPG structure, crappy UI interactions especially on my controller.

<-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------->

12 hours in, the translation quality fell down a lot after the 2nd story module but having the tolerance of reading MTL, I liked what I played especially the 3rd story module because of the openness I also played the text only story module and somehow I think the icons to indicate choices becomes really confusing since I don't exactly know which choice wants me to go forward at times was still a fun experience if you like reading though like I said the translation quality. 

Speaking of translation, lots of text boxes especially on the mythical item descriptions, the texts does not fit and end up not being understandable, another main problem I had was where I have a character that is "Severely Injured" which is a "Madness" trait and the description was that the character is stuck on max hp of 6 and this condition could supposedly be dormant if the character heals on the interlude now I don't know what they meant by that because I've brought her to the hospital and a private sanitarium on the in between parts and I'm just confused why it's still there I just wish these parts can be communicated better.


<bugs I found?>
the clunky UI were rarely a problem but it can be confusing to first time players, one of my first playthroughs actually had this bug where I cannot open the menu so I just assumed it was impossible at the start of the module, another bug I got was when I defeated [spoiler] Tindalos [/spoiler] blank text boxes from the [spoiler] 3 characters, my character, Saya, and Shirley(Sherry?) [/spoiler] was blocking the screen and I wasn't able to view the ending properly without looking in the back log

comment_evidence.full_review:
终于狠狠打通了谎言与欺诈的he赶来评价一下（被揍得死去活来疯狂sl

本质上其实玩起来还是感觉更像多线rpg不过制作很精良也很上头！！
但是调查员打架的时间未免太多，相比起探索大部分时候都在为了思索怎么打死怪和被骰子暴打的情况下维护岌岌可危的那一点点生命值。。哪有调查员天天直面古神啊！
谁懂，我每次一看见有不得了的东西就快吓死了。。哦内该少一点战斗。。。多关爱脸黑调查员的小身板。。。
而且这骰子的沉度导致做个东西经常失败（然而事实上很多材料获取又非常困难陷入的痛苦sl，属实是降低游戏体验，毕竟没有一个活的kp可以物理说服（目移）
以及在本游里好像幸运值和精神值都变成一种纯粹技能消耗点数了，感觉其实可以有更多发挥（？
（依稀记得以前因为精神值降低队友疯狂起来哐哐砸死全队友直接结团的经历）
呜呜呜本来以为可以捏人的，本pc爱好者流下了眼泪、、
还有虽然是调查员们，但本质只有亚南吧亚南！

总之就是再玩不到完整版我要死了！！！！

------------

卡森德拉一周目打通了，现在的人格解体各方面都挺完善的，最直观的感受就是在场景里用各种理由塞了超级多能吃能用小垃圾哈哈哈哈，一圈打下来背包里好多页（尤其是卡镇）。
本体就很耐玩，而且由于有创意工坊的存在此游戏基本能一直玩下去（感谢每个付出的老师）
至于战斗方面有mod和官方死亡回溯至少不会卡关，出现了，这个物理伤害爆炸的世界！
而且npc完全是战神我好爱，解决我的许多烦恼，希望以后出更多剧本职业神话物品dlc和新的角色模型或者捏人！！pc爱好者真的很需要这个

comment_evidence.clause: this game is very DND inspired with dice checks in combat and object/environment interaction with elements of the Chtulhu mythos but mainly about aberrant supernatural horrors
comment_evidence.full_review:
i only really cleared 2 modules, the prologue and the first module that was under it but was still captivated by the game

what really stands out about the game is the story and rpg elements of the game. you get put into self contained stories that you try to figure out with your player characters. this game is very DND inspired with dice checks in combat and object/environment interaction with elements of the Chtulhu mythos but mainly about aberrant supernatural horrors. one of the biggest mechanic of the game is the event decisions you make which will determine what ending you will get that becomes based off your choices and what you do. this game actively encourages you to explore and try out different choices that you may not have chosen at the beginning. I highly suggest to use the save and load function and the game feels like it wants us to use the save and load feature to our upmost capabilities because sometimes failing a dice check or succeeding a dice check will change entirely on what will happen, for example failing a check you may not enocunter this one enemy npc but succeeding a check will have you detect the enemy npc and engage in a fight. enemy encounters in combat is also quite complex with several actions with a given % of success. this game very DND inspired in dice checking for several different enoucouters and combat actoins. typically each action you want to attempt comes with a dice roll or check based on your characters abilities. 
the game is separated into what the call modules or pretty much self contained rpg stories that  is connected to the game through the central game lobby hub area where you create new player characters(investigators) and gear them up. AFter clearing modules depending on what you find there are certain mythic items and titles you keep from clearing the module and achieving an ending to the module. and your PC can equip the diffrent items and titles. these titles give buffs/debuffs too
the art and music bgm for the different locations and also during enemy counters are actually really good. I really enjoy the art style of the characters despite most of the game being in pixel esque graphics. 

another feature of the game is the ability to create your own modules, so you can create your own level and story which is pretty cool if you into more creative side of the things, and there are currently a bunch of chinese made modules made by players that are popular but dont have an official translation to therm 

side note this was made by an indie chinese developer and a noticed a few minor translation issues in grammar but they are actively working with a translation team to fix these problems,

TLDR lovely story inspired by cthulu mythos. explore and investigate surroundings, DND style checks and turn based combat, personalized PC you can create and equip for diversity, player made stories included, lovely art and gfx, great bgm track

Put in a lot of effort to master the mechanics of the dive jump, the timing of the difficult enemies, then get killed by a hidden trap.  Which sets you back out of the area you worked so hard to clear. 
 
The visuals are great and what I saw of the story is cool but the artificial difficulty makes it impossible to enjoy all the other elements and one is left perpetually annoyed.   
 
Games which are intentionally stupidly difficult like Getting Over It (which I loved) or the Hollow Knight's Pantheon (which I also loved) are fun because that's the entire premise.  It's all about training and mastery. 
 
Here, it's just tedious.

comment_evidence.clause: I learned the void attacks pretty darn well and was just able to wallop her while she did extended cast animations instead of frame perfect parries and flips
comment_evidence.full_review:
Split original review into comments now that I have finished the game (100%, passing of ages, filled out hunter's journal, just under 60 hours on my save file) and collected my thoughts.

---

Silksong does improve on core mechanics of HK while adding much more agility to the player kit, and combat is much more engaging and varied than in the first game. That being said, the game is designed to be played by strictly following the quest line, in order. A lot of the interesting area's in Silksong have limited rewards or are just extremely hidden. I got annoyed pretty quickly in act 3 when I started having to just spam my super jump into random ceilings. A lot of the requirements for act 3, along with the quest markers for the act + finding lost fleas, are also purposefully misleading. Looking around online, I was not the only person who thought the Flea Caravan stopped at the Grand Gate or that the Heart of the Woods would have an entrance in, you know, the woods, especially since it is marked directly above said  woods AND you just got a vertical traversal ability.

EXPLORATION:
With the difficulty curve being closely tied to the quest line, there are several paths you can take that feel like they are purposefully put there to punish you for exploring early. The gauntlet in Hunter's March (with 5 masks, no dash, no tools) and the Sinner's Path -> Bilewater entrance that can be reached without clawline or double jump while the player has a +0 to +1 pin and a measly 6-7 masks are two particularly atrocious examples of areas that punish you for exploring "too early." While you could just simply leave, the punishing economy in this game (I know it was worse on release) forces you to try and get your money back from whatever locked arena or miserable poison pit you died in, driving you further into frustration and tedium. And again, its worth mentioning the middling rewards many zones / boss fights provide.

COMBAT:
As good as combat feels, TC decided to go way overboard with flying enemies to counteract Hornet's movement + the addition of tools. There are far too many gauntlets, with some being forgettable while some are harder than most boss fights (depending on when you reach them), and they can completely interrupt the flow of the game.

Regardless of anyone's opinion on Silksong, I have yet to come across a single two mask contact damage defender. For such a dexterous game, having (almost) every boss deal two contact damage feels overly punishing rather than interesting, and, again, becomes tedious once you reach the bosses that can teleport right into you.

By the end of my 100% + hunter's journal run, I also realized very few enemies, or even bosses, have unique attacks. A majority of act 3 bosses utilize the triple dash attack you have been dealing with since the ants in Hunter's March. I genuinely think a big reason a lot of the bosses can feel too easy for more proficient players or just plain old forgettable is because a lot of them lack a unique kit or identity. Many fights are also incredibly prolonged via ranged / AOE spam and flying out of reach (I'm looking at you, Pinstress and Nyleth, the latter primarily because of her annoying hitbox transitions during her animations that make pogoing annoying).

LATE GAME / HEAVY SPOILERS:
Additionally, while I understand the reasoning for the void cursed enemies in act 3, having LITRALLY ANY enemy triple their health, start dealing two contact damage, draining silk, and gaining one of four random AOE attacks gets really old, really quick. Even if you clear the void nest things, any enemy you fight can become way tankier before the transform animation has even started, breaking up the late game backtracking / traversal in the same way gauntlets broke up the early game's pacing (sometimes for the worse).

Going back to unique boss fights, I also found Lost Lace's phase two much easier than her phase one since, while going for my hunter's journal 100%, I learned the void attacks pretty darn well and was just able to wallop her while she did extended cast animations instead of frame perfect parries and flips.

Short but important mention: To have GMS and LL be the two final boss fights of the much awaited HK sequel is a let down.

SUMMARY:
I don't know. I don't feel like diving back into Silksong because I'm worried I'll miss x, y, or z secret path that I have totally forgotten about since the map is pretty huge. A lot of the boss fights felt over or under tuned, depending on when you encounter them and your playstyle, and I think a really important part of game design is making sure the players can explore the map in a natural way without being overly punished. There were a couple memorable fights, but I don't feel driven or compelled to try and reach them again. Overall, the game is a solid 6/10 and I'm sure when I come back eventually to play again (steel soul + speedruns) or for the DLC, I will enjoy it more now that I know what to avoid and when to go there. But to make a souls-like / Metroidvania, two genres that both heavily feature "hard area you can get early," feel this punishing for so many fans of the franchise / genres definitely rubs me the wrong way. I'm glad Silksong isn't just more Hollow Knight and that the game has a unique identity, I just wish the game wasn't designed to be so purposefully frustrating for players who love to explore, and that more love and care went into the boss fights given how bonkers Hornet's combat capabilities are.

Like many others who have finished Silksong (went for 100%, all endings, hunter's journal), I'm more so glad it's over for now.

comment_evidence.clause: * no ingame health bar for bosses (or visual indications like wounds or changing colors) to keep track on how good you performed and close it was
comment_evidence.full_review:
Silksong is a big enhancement over the first game, but repeats the same concept mistakes.

[table][tr][td]
Overall      ★★★★★★★☆☆☆ - 7/10
Music        ★★★★★★★★☆☆ - 8/10
Graphics   ★★★★★★★★☆☆ - 8/10
Gameplay ★★★★★★★☆☆☆ - 7/10
Story         ★★★★★☆☆☆☆☆ - 5/10
[/td][/tr][/table]

Difficulty   ★★★★☆☆☆☆☆☆ (normal game mode, steel mode is hardcore gamer exclusive)

[b]What did I like?[/b]

* better main protagonist
* big lovely created world that is fun to explore
* cool boss fights which are in fact readable this time, so it is always a preparation and skill thing to beat them
* graphic style is not so boring as in the first game
* the different crest add a lot of replayability
* the world is not as confusing to discover like in the first game
* cutscenes
* overall good quality

[b]What did I not like?[/b]

* no NG+
* no difficulty settings but just a senseless perma-death game mode only for hardcore gamers
* soulslike elements like bonfire and recollect your stuff if you died
* checkpoints (benches) are often too far away from the bossfights (no direct replay and requip function if you died)
* difficulty of steel mode is just a too big leap, one time just bad luck and you have to start over
* too much kaizo platforming parts, but less frustrating than in HK1
* no ingame health bar for bosses (or visual indications like wounds or changing colors) to keep track on how good you performed and close it was
* a lot of interesting items that you will never use due to too few slots
* while there is that farsight item, there is no ingame help to find missed secrets, you need external sources (bad)

[b]Red flags or what did I hate?[/b]

The main things that are (still) bothering me is that Team Cherry added again soulslike elements, and trophies exclusively for hardcore gamers. To force players to do those hardcore game modes (speaking of Steel mode, speedrunning it in less than 5 hours or 100% the game in less than 30 hours as well) to get trophies is a slap into a lot of gamers faces. Seeing the percentage of those trophies I am pretty much sure a lot of players just cheesed or cheated it. The percentage is by far not realistic because it is very very difficult and frustrating to achieve.

Speaking of the Steel mode, it is a waste of time. If someone really wants to speedrun or play perma-death, he will, there is no need to add an extra mode or trophies for it. Everyone can just delete his savegame if he died and start over by himself. I would have liked that Team Cherry concentrated on more valuable features instead.

I still don't understand the value of the soulslike elements like bonfire and recollecting stuff features, having to run from a faraway bench for hundreds of times to redo a boss fight is just annoying. Not letting the player just decide 'ok, boss is too hard for the moment I come back later' but I need to recollect my stuff again, and sometimes even are not possible to without triggering the boss fight again is just bad game design. And Team Cherry knew that it s*cked and added items to work around it rather than just get rid of it. Very disappointing.

The game also feels more like work, not fun if you go for all trophies or 100% the game. This is a basic problem the game series has. I guess the devs will make this mistake in upcoming games as well. Because if this I will always hesitate to play this game again rather than just hop in.

[b]Conclusion:[/b]

In my opinion Silksong is definitely better in everything than its predecessor. Especially the boss fights are way more readable making them actually fun (still demanding yet not frustrating). And thus the story is now good enough so that I can understand and follow the reasoning of our heroine I feel now appealed to it. 

Still, I don't believe that the soulslike elements are fitting for this game. And adding kaizo jumping and senseless game modes solely for hardcore gamers kill the accessibility and joy for causal or even regular gamers as well. Team Cherry should definitely get rid of that.

While I consider the game still is still a rather good game, I can only recommend this game to a very small audience, most players can or should skip it. No fomo here.

[b]PS:[/b] Ah yes, Team Cherry, you still owe me money for my game controller I destroyed during my first game out of frustration due to your furiating gameplay mechanics. Contact me to settle things.

comment_evidence.full_review:
10/10

Gameplay: 9.5/10
Bosses: 9.5/10
Music: 10/10
Story: 9.5/10
Exploration/secrets: 9.5/10
Art/Design: 10/10

Absolute masterpiece. Overall i would say that it's at least as good as the first game in all aspects, and it much better in some of them. It is also a huge game, with almost twice as many locations as the first game.

Within the first couple of hours i was really annoyed at the change to the heal system, going from incremental by 1 mask in Hollow Knight to only being able to heal 3 masks at a time in this game, as well as the diagonal pogo being a bit awkward but that's a skill issue. But as soon as you get 1-2 additional masks missing 2-3 before being able to heal becomes not as bad(almost all bossed deal double damage so if you have 5 masks and wait to lose 3 before heal, you are 1-hit from dying), and by the late game it actually makes the game easier than the first one because you can heal mid-air and you can equip a charm to heal faster, which let's you heal on most attacks of most bosses, which is not at all the case in the first game for the last couple of bosses. 

The charm system is different from the first game, and i really respect that, especially considering how many metroidvanias have since adoptad that system. The new one is maybe a little less flexible, but at the same time by the end of the game you can equip more charms than in the first game, even thought they can't be all offensive or defensive. The ability to change your needle range/speed and heal system is also nice, even though i barely changed to anything other than the reaper crest which was the first new one i got after the default. I also like that charms here are quite a bit more balanced without standout ones that you basically always want to wear like the first game. The addition of tools was also really cool, and poisonous cogfiles carried me through a lot of unpleasant situations, though i almost didn't use them on the hardest bosses because they distracted me from attack patterns.

I really like hornet's moveset, it's a step up in complexity from the first game and it really shows in the mid-late game platforming sections that were a lot of fun to beat. The ability to sprint is a big quality of life improvement, and all the animations are so smooth that movement feels very pleasant in this game when you do it right.

Bosses here are definitely a step up from the first game, in difficulty as well as design and versatility. There were a bit too many bosses that summon normal enemies for my liking in the early game, but as soon as you reach widow it's just banger after banger from then on, at least for the main story bosses. Side quest and secret bosses were also quite cool, and i even managed to miss a couple without knowing.

Exploration was great here, with maps being generally accessible pretty early into each area which i appreciate(let's not talk how i didn't know that Shakra returns to the village and you can buy maps there and thus ran through all of shellwood without a map). There are a ton of secrets, ranging from charms to mask/spool upgrades to optional bosses and sometimes even completely optional areas.

Storywise for me this was a huge step up from the first game. Hollow knight story was very mysterious, but in the end lore didn't affect the gameplay too much. In this game however the protagonist can actually talk and has a personality, which for me made npc interactions much more impactful, as well as other story elements such as worlds progression. And the true ending... it is just absolute cinema, i loved it so much.

comment_evidence.clause: I was pretty disappointed it was not within the genre I had assigned it in my mind however I was getting wrapped up in the story and the gameplay/graphics are surprisingly good so I figured I'd keep playing
comment_evidence.full_review:
I got Indika from a Bundle, I knew nothing going in and out of the games I got within the bundle, Indika was quickly forgotten about within my library. Fast forward however long later and I was looking for something to play and the art caught my eye, plus the weed sounding name XD. I seen it was marked as "horror" and with the religious description & trailer, I was getting a lot of Faith/Cultic/Outlast vibes and I figured I'd give it a shot. I was pretty disappointed it was not within the genre I had assigned it in my mind however I was getting wrapped up in the story and the gameplay/graphics are surprisingly good so I figured I'd keep playing.

Indika is a weird one. The game brings up a lot of questions and philosophy which I liked, Puzzles were hard enough to make you think, But not hard enough to make you look up a walkthrough. Its a good one time play, But its not a re-playable type game. Id rate it a solid 6.7/10 and I feel thats pretty solid tbh. I dont regret playing it, and I enjoyed it - I just think its a bit lackluster looking back on it. But with a 3ish hour time to beat? Its a decent way to spend a night.

comment_evidence.clause: It feels like they made a beautiful 90minute movie-like narrative experience and then added in some puzzle elements and the pixel graphic mini games to pad it out to be a "complete" game
comment_evidence.full_review:
It is great and terrible all at the same time. 

The opening sequence really wowed me with cinematography, music, surrealism and really set the tone....which is then ruined by sections of a completely different art style and gameplay from the main experience. Mind you the pixel art is beautiful, it's just really out of place and takes away from the direction of the main narrative and direction. It feels like they made a beautiful 90minute movie-like narrative experience and then added in some puzzle elements and the pixel graphic mini games to pad it out to be a "complete" game. 

I would compare it to Hellblade:Senua's Sacrifice but it falls short due to the negatives taking away from that type of experience. 

Get it on a deep deep discount and treat it like a movie - stick to the on rails experience, don't explore and just go through it in 3 hours or less. (it would be an incredible movie btw if  you take away all the minimal game elements here)

comment_evidence.clause: 16-bit flashback scenes and UI are pleasant to look at although initially a little confusing on a design scale as the game’s more realistic presentation everywhere else doesn’t allude to these whimsical diatribes
comment_evidence.full_review:
I’ll be up front: you’re not going to play another game like INDIKA this year.  Sure there will be other third person adventure games largely rooted in story-related set pieces and light puzzle mechanics to break the walking simulator aspects that will pop up on your catered game store page of choice, but they’re not going to be like INDIKA.  

Set in the outskirts of Russia in the 19th century, you play as Indika, a monastery nun outcast by her compatriots for past indications we learn later in the game, and also her wild instances around others based on her internal struggle with a voice inside her head, the voice of the Devil.  Indika is given a letter to provide to another church leader that calls her to traverse across towns but is sent on an unexpected adventure draped in self-discovery and sobering questions regarding the morality of religion and the balance of free will and heavenly expectations.

INDIKA starts with an over-the-shoulder perspective going through daily chores, done almost as a penalty than a necessity, giving the player a front row seat in the uselessness and unnecessary nature of the tasks.  Taking a basket of potatoes from one part of the village to another with no thanks, having to walk back and forth several meters to fill a barrel with water from a well, using each keystroke to begrudgingly turn the crank, only to finish the task with an elder dumping it all out.  No respect given, but respect is expected to be earned.

Past experiences where Indika has inadvertently put herself in this scenario are peppered in this slowly-paced intro, highlighting some real off-beat, slightly confusing, but chuckle-inducing cutscenes where you get a front row view of what Indika is having to deal with while maintaining her stoic status.  The pixelated, 16-bit flashback scenes and UI are pleasant to look at although initially a little confusing on a design scale as the game’s more realistic presentation everywhere else doesn’t allude to these whimsical diatribes.  Is this Indika’s representation of a more fantastical world before being succumbed to the lowly drudges of an emotionless standard?

Indika can perform godly tasks, such as lighting lamps draped with images of Christ and praying for the recently deceased, giving Indika “points.”  These points are used to “level up” with skills such as Guilt and Repentance.  It’s a tongue-in-cheek way to show that people will use the continuous need of doing things for their religion to internally level up and feel like they’re reaching a higher point in their beliefs: but the game will flat out tell you they’re worth nothing.  Karl Marx will agree as well.

Once she is given the letter to present to another church leader, the world opens up to a blustery winter landscape and our adventure truly begins.  Indika is soon attached to Ilya, a prison escapee who is looking for divine intervention to repair his frostbitten, mangled arm.  Ilya takes Indika hostage and forces her to escape with him while she pilots a steam-powered bicycle in what has to be the funniest chase sequence I’ve seen in years.  Monty Python aficionados would be proud at the ridiculousness and pure comedy of this moment and gets you in a great set of laughs in between the bleakness of the surrounding travel.

Because going forward, INDIKA puts the realizations and hypocrisies of specific parts of religious happenings to light and in turn, putting Indika in a state of teetering belief and splitting guilt.  Fighting the other side of her arguments literally splits her psyche in two, retreating to muttered prayers to temporarily fix her tempted ways.  INDIKA uses this mental anguish to introduce small puzzles while your internal Devil birades your attempts to ground yourself.  It’s a very cool mechanic that sadly isn’t used often, but is remembered fondly when it did show up.

INDIKA spends most of its time outside of cutscenes and plot advancing to break the tension with smaller puzzles.  Puzzles range from building puzzles, to navigation, to…uh, maneuvering past a massive dog-wolf being looking to make you a human chew toy?  None of the puzzles are too hard but are satisfying enough to finish and are a nice break in the walking simulator path the game takes when not putting the square peg in front of the circle slot.  It’s worth noting that INDIKA’s use of camera and perceived angles, especially as truths are slotted in front of Indika and the world before her is started to be seen in a different light in the third act are some of the smartest I’ve witnessed in a long time.  The use of different perspectives on a point of view level left my mouth agape as it defined what it meant without even saying a word.

The story clocks in at a tight 3-4 hours but never feels like it overstays its welcome.  Though there really isn’t much in terms of replayability, you don’t really need it for this: it’s telling its story and you’re here to indulge.  I did run into some minor slowdown in the more popular areas that really did not enjoy motion blur, even on turned-down graphical settings.  I was really jazzed to play INDIKA in its natural Russian language, but text used within the world is not subtitled nor is the small talk from other characters, so I moved back to English to avoid missing anything, which the English voice actors did a damn fine job in and of itself, so I have no complaints other than missing out on some wanted authenticity.

INDIKA is a weird game to score because it is, like said above, nothing like you’ve played before.  It’s proudly weird but grounded in its reasons to be, laugh-out-loud funny and despairingly somber on the flip of a coin, and just long enough to get its deeply rooted point simultaneously into your heart and your brain.  Odd Meter and 11bit studios embrace a topic often left alone, but the glory of Video Games are that you can take concepts as silly, in-depth, depressing, enlightening, eye-opening, soul-crushing as the ones provided in INDIKA and with enough heart and tenacity to do so, you can create a near masterpiece.

comment_evidence.clause: but the artstyle and atmosphere provided by it is so hauntingly beautiful in a way that really gets you to like the characters and go through the story without having to look away as you anticipate a jumpscare
comment_evidence.full_review:
As someone who doesn't do well with contextual language learning, this was still a fun game to play!! I love the concept of having to progress through the story by learning an entirely new language, and I personally made the experience more fun for myself my using my own language to fill in the dictionary, which somehow made my guesses both more accurate (probably) and more funny in retrospect!! 
 
I love horror as a genre, but personally can't play horror games. This game wasn't necessarily scary, but the artstyle and atmosphere provided by it is so hauntingly beautiful in a way that really gets you to like the characters and go through the story without having to look away as you anticipate a jumpscare. I can't remember how many endings there were in total, but there were at least 18 numbered endings (I'm sure there's more!!) And you can enjoy the story blindly (if you're only interested in "dating" the characters), or get fully immersed in the story of trying to find out what the Umbrella guy's deal with you is without having to really skimp on the storytelling. 
 
Whether you're playing this to find out everyone's goal, or you're just here for the appeal of the characters/atmosphere of the game, you will not be disappointed playing this game!! Truly is a fun and stimulating experience that will make you laugh (oddly enough) and scratch at your head as you learn the new language.

comment_evidence.clause: there are quick time events which is always a fun thing to see in visual novels because it whips the player out of reading and fills them with adrenaline to be able to react fast which adds to the horror aspect
comment_evidence.full_review:
Great game but please add a cloud save feature :-:

Edit: I'll try to make this review as spoiler-free as possible and specifically state SPOILER when it can't be helped and END when the spoiler is over.

Now that I've finished the entire game and obtained all the endings and CGs, I can say that this is not a full on otome game in the traditional sense. Their are routes but the endings are left ambiguous besides the fact that they're stuck with you because of the situation. The routes happen based on your choices so it's not like you get to pick a man or woman. You're genuinely just trying to survive and then making bad choices to spend more time with them instead of leaving TO SAFETY. 

But, that's okay, because I thought that's where the romance aspect was going to kick in. WRONG! There's only two men who specifically state they love/like you after you've deciphered the vocabulary of course. 
SPOILERS, it's Mr. Scarlettella and Mr. Crawling. Mr. Gap just wants you for your body... body parts :-:. Mr. Scarletella is trying to take your soul so Mr. Crawling is left as the only good option and as far as I know the only ghost that can come live with you happily in the real world. END 

The puzzle part of the game is interesting because I haven't really seen many games where you can decipher a language. In the beginning of the game, it's not that important to understand the language but it is later on because Mr. Gap is an issue... Also, there are quick time events which is always a fun thing to see in visual novels because it whips the player out of reading and fills them with adrenaline to be able to react fast which adds to the horror aspect. 

IN CONCLUSION, this game truly is more like a horror, adventure visual novel where you're trying to survive with some romance aspects. But, you will never go past smiling, being next to each other, or patting each other's heads. So do not buy this if you're looking for a purely romantic otome game with some horror aspects because it's the opposite. This game is going to throw you back and forth through an unintelligible hell if you don't try to put in the work to decipher the language. 

There's a prologue available for free because the devs were kind enough so I highly suggest any interested players in playing that before deciding if they want to buy this game.

comment_evidence.clause: It's just a well made arcade style game with a cute aesthetic that you can keep going back to as they add new content without feeling like you have to start over or miss out
comment_evidence.full_review: I don't usually buy into early access games. But there's just something about dungeon clawer. It's just a simple and fun, easily accessible and a great time waster to play while listening to some background noise. The 1 campaign in the game takes about 30-40 mins for a play through depending on the RNG and what kind of build you end up with. But where it lacks in distance dungeon clawer makes up for in volume. There's many characters to unlock with different passives and decks, rabbit feet to collect (new passives) by beating a run with each character, secret characters to unlock during a run, different builds and strats to try out, etc. The replayability is what's keeping me interested and playing for almost 10 hours now. So if this is your type of game and you're wondering if it's worth the price, it definitely is! It's just a well made arcade style game with a cute aesthetic that you can keep going back to as they add new content without feeling like you have to start over or miss out. Would definitely recommend!

comment_evidence.clause: I would like more information on certain things like status effects that I can hover over using a gamepad though (works great on Steam Deck btw)
comment_evidence.full_review:
I'm absolutely hooked on this game, I can't believe I've already put 16 hours into it. I don't know where the time has gone. It combines two of my favorite things; roguelikes and claw machines, and it does it well. Controlling and aiming the claw feels great and I don't have any complaints about the physics. I would like more information on certain things like status effects that I can hover over using a gamepad though (works great on Steam Deck btw). I'm surprised this is still early access as it really feels pretty complete, so I'm looking forward to whatever gets added or updated. This is a must buy if it sounds fun to you, no need to wait for a full release.

*Edit July 18 2025: I could have sworn this was out of early access! I loved this from the beginning and since then there has been SO much more content added, it's nuts. It has just kept improving and it's a rare game I keep coming back to and 8 months later I'm still getting hooked on it. I'm really impressed by the progress.

*Edit May 20th 2026: I could have sworn this left Early Access like 3 times, but no, it was less than a month ago. They just keep adding more content. Great game, love it, buy it.

comment_evidence.clause: There are some balance issues since some synergies don't pay off nearly as well as others and I found normal to have been the hardest difficulty because extra claw effects are so powerful
comment_evidence.full_review:
Oh goodness, there goes my free time!


11/29/24 Edit: At 35ish hours (A majority of it was just left running while paused) I've 100%ed the EA. By this I mean all characters on nightmare, I did not do any major endless runs, but I feel I understand the scaling well enough now that I could take it as far as possible with strength or coin scaling.

There are some balance issues since some synergies don't pay off nearly as well as others and I found normal to have been the hardest difficulty because extra claw effects are so powerful.

I recently completed Luck Be A Landlord and Balatro and this game was much easier to get to the "end". Though that could be due to my recent time in those games helping me think about the strats and improve.

Overall, I still recommend it and am excited to see what gets added in future updates, what I'd like to see more of is mechanics that inspire emergent game play strategies (maybe through cross-material interactions) and maybe more ways to "interact" with your items (both in game and remove/improve/alchemy-wise). 

I know it's a claw game, but when you hit points where you cannot win due to having to "blindly" dig for an item at the bottom of a pile it does not feel great. So maybe something like personal TV-head bombs to shake up your items. Or maybe like 1-2 "machine shakes/hits" per run for getting you out of a bind.

comment_evidence.clause: The technical upgrades go beyond just improved visuals (which are gorgeous) and introduce stronger underlying systems that enable more creative puzzles and deeper interaction with the environments
comment_evidence.full_review:
I was a big fan of Escape Simulator, and this sequel smashes it out of the park. The technical upgrades go beyond just improved visuals (which are gorgeous) and introduce stronger underlying systems that enable more creative puzzles and deeper interaction with the environments.

One of the best things about ES is that even once you finish the included campaigns, the devs are forever releasing bonus content. After finishing the main campaigns, there are free rooms to play and reasonably priced DLC. The developers even continue to add bonus content and improvements to the first game, which is almost unheard of once a sequel is made. On top of that, there’s an active community creating and sharing high-quality custom rooms for free.

comment_evidence.clause: The puzzles are good and the environments look nice but there are some things about the original game that make this one feel a little more empty and sterile
comment_evidence.full_review:
Having played all of Escape Sim 1 I will start by saying that the fact that you cannot equip hats you find in this game is really disappointing. The charm seems a bit lost compared to the first. It also seems like the escape rooms are more geared towards single player gameplay as I often found myself or my friend standing around while one of us figures out the puzzle in a room. In the first game it felt more balanced and we didnt find ourselves waiting around as much as with this one.
The puzzles are good and the environments look nice but there are some things about the original game that make this one feel a little more empty and sterile. Over all I'm happy with it but seeing that the splash art on the steam page was very obviously done with Ai is very disappointing so I'm hesitant to throw more money at it. 
If you enjoyed the first game then you'll probably enjoy this one just be aware that its less charming than the first.

comment_evidence.clause: graphics became realistic and it is downside because now there are more details that steal your attention (my ADHD wife suffers lol) and some puzzles became pretty boring
comment_evidence.full_review:
[h1] Escape Simulator 2: A Rough Continuation [/h1]

My wife and I beat the first game fully, sometimes playing community-made levels, so I would say we are pretty fond of this game as we both like puzzles.

I can't say it is better than the first game, imho the first game was better at almost everything: UI is more pretty, the UI of the second game seems like a browser RPG from noughties; graphics became realistic and it is downside because now there are more details that steal your attention (my ADHD wife suffers lol) and some puzzles became pretty boring. BUT new game engine offers us new puzzles too. They became more complex and sometimes even mind-breaking to us.

I think, Pine Studio rushed the release of the game, that's why it looks very Early Access-ish, like those cheap Unity games from 2010s. I hope they will take their time and fix optimization of the game, polish the UI and then it will be a good continuation to our beloved Escape Simulator

comment_evidence.clause: clue quality is worse (with a misleading animation in a room telling you the complete opposite of what you need to do)
comment_evidence.full_review:
having played through every room in Escape Simulator 1, including all DLC, i was really looking forward to this sequel, and although it is fun, it ultimately feels like a downgrade from the original.

multiplayer is buggy (with random disconnects and sync issues), clue quality is worse (with a misleading animation in a room telling you the complete opposite of what you need to do), and a puzzle in the lobby that seems accessible to regular players, but deliberately breaks the usual escape room rules that will lead to players trying to solve a puzzle they can't do without exterior knowledge.

on a more positive note, the Darkest Puzzles are an interesting addition, and help expand on some previously learnt skills, and the room themes are also nice, making the most of creating scenarios that wouldn't otherwise be able to exist outside of a video game.

this is still a fun game, but i would highly recommend anyone new to the series playing the original and all DLC first before touching this.
