comment_evidence.clause: however I really feel like they desperately need another set of eyes looking over so many design choices - mostly in terms of interface and graphics - that lead to major frustrations
comment_evidence.full_review:
My experience summarised; spent 20 minutes trying to work out a puzzle only for my cooperative partner to move one piece, have the puzzle INSTANTLY drastically change rule-sets and structure before my very eyes, and become instantly solvable.  If that sounds frustrating to you, come back to this game in a however-long.

And now, in full:

I love Escape Simulator very deeply, and I've played every room I could with my partner - all the DLCs, plenty of community rooms, and while there's been moments of frustrations with certain puzzle logic, I've never quite experienced "rulebreaking" in the rooms to the degree that Escape Simulator 2 suffers.

Sometimes items don't function until your partner picks them up.  Sometimes solving a puzzle doesn't work until your partner steps over and interacts with it, forcefully readjusting whatever desync you've been suffering up until then.  Sometimes you don't even see the item or puzzle they're gesturing towards.  Several puzzles I attempted in Dracula's Castle seemed to have drastically different results based on the timing of when I clicked things, providing further and further desync that made finding the intended solution literally impossible.  Sure I could "bruteforce" the answer by using this glitch, but...  why would I want that?

There's growing pains to be sure, but I have to say the massive new visual direction taken in the latest entry also does nothing for me.  Characters in the previous game, although basic, were very iconic, and the clean, low detail art style made everything spring forward in an identifiable and clear way - kind of like how Portal, for example, featured that sort of faux-corporate scifi cleanliness to everything that also functioned as keeping the visual language of the game simple?  Now the noise and clutter of every scene leaves me- an admittedly very easy to overwhelm person- kind of at a complete loss as to how to approach rooms.  Characters are sort of stuck in a weird uncanny valley of looking too detailed to hold to a style, but too clunky, ugly, and poorly animated to be anything but rigid, personality-less dummies.  Why do I need incredibly detailed facial features and animations if I can't actually customise those elements of myself?

On top of which, as far as I've progressed, the puzzles all seem to be linear in such a way that cooperation is usually discouraged.  Multiple times I or my partner have been "-this- close" to solving something, leaving the other simply standing on the sidelines waiting for things to click into place.  Gone are the days you could sort of "meet in the middle" with your various tasks, now a lot of your time will be spent simply twiddling your thumbs and waiting- and lord help you if you're trying a room with more than two people.  Eight players?!

At the end of the day, I'm happy with my purchase to support the developers, and I'm glad they've made a sequel.  Outside of that enthusiasm for the continued development-...  I really do not have anything really positive to say about my time in ES2.  I found myself wanting to ask my partner if we could go back to the first game and find some community rooms we hadn't done yet, and that's a terrible sign for the remaining levels in the sequel.

Can all of this be fixed?  Well, potentially, yes- and I'm very willing to review this review as we continue, and as these problems are patched- but I still can't help but think of what was left behind in the original game.  Perhaps as community rooms begin to pop up and the new, apparently more powerful level editor gets flexed a little more, I'll change my tune.

Maybe this negative opinion is all just desync.

EDIT: Hi!  Checking in.  This review was written during Dracula's Castle, and this update is being added after clearing the next outer space levels.

There are a LOT more promising levels in the next section and I do appreciate them, however I really feel like they desperately need another set of eyes looking over so many design choices - mostly in terms of interface and graphics - that lead to major frustrations.  A good example happens early on; there's a block puzzle featuring a sort of series of "plug" and "outlet" symbology.  Logically speaking, you'd place plugs into outlets to fit them together, right?  Well...  No!  Apparently the solve is to make sure that all the plugs plug into plugs.  Because that...  completes the plug.  I guess.

The same room features an audio based puzzle where you must dice recorded voice lines into a certain passphrase to unlock a door.  Theoretically, I love this - I'm a former podcaster, streamer, and I do audio engineering and editing for both work and fun pretty much all the time.  This puzzle is a nightmare because it features captions that don't line up even remotely with what's being said, and the solve seems to want you to clip parts of the audio that aren't even close to the actual syllables and sounds you're meant to be cutting.  I got the answer by feeling out "what I think the game wants from me" rather than, satisfyingly, actually putting the puzzle together.

This is one of those "I think the rules are unintuitive" moments that curses basically every room at least once, sometimes multiple times, and my assumption is a lot of it is flexing what new depth they can add to the puzzles.  That part's commendable; there's tons of really ambitious puzzles that maybe wouldn't have worked perfectly in the original game featured, but...  when the answer is apparent, whether solved by me or hinted at by the game, the rewarding moment of "ah!  I get it now!" seems to have been mostly replaced with "oh, wow, the symbology/design/tutorial for this was misleading (or directly wrong)."

This is especially obvious in a later puzzle that features an endlessly replaying tutorial video that cannot be disabled or moved aside directly on top of the puzzle.  If you, like me, assume that the endlessly replaying sequence is somehow key to the puzzle due to its particular timings, inability to be moved or disabled, and endless repetition, you will be stuck here.  It's actually just a video of a completely different sequence to show you the rules of the puzzle - in theory very helpful, but its placement, obtrusiveness, and connected nature will probably lead you to a very different conclusion.

It's really strange; room to room we're having totally different experiences.  Where there isn't one of these huge clarity issues, we're clearing rooms with 20-25+ minutes remaining on the timer, because when the puzzles themselves are clear they're all mostly very, very simple, honestly sometimes really disappointing in how little they utilize their own premise.  You'll interpret the first panel of a puzzle as "the teaching one," where it shows you the logic and then expands it into its own mini-game or series of functions, and it's...  not.  It just ends.

Which brings up something I've wanted to rant about; the "resync" button.  It's wonderful that you've put resyncing in the players hands!  I think that's a great addition of a button to help alleviate desync issues.  However, I'd like to pose a thought exercise; how would you ever know to press that button?

How, genuinely, is a player meant to know they're desynced?  Any sort of realistic scenario would be ideal.  I get that the button exists because the problem persists, but how is it meant to be used?  How am I meant to know the puzzle pieces I'm looking at don't fit together?  Should I just intermittently "resync" and throw my partner out of whatever task or puzzle they're doing because I 'got the vibe it's impossible?'

I have no idea how I'll update this review further as this is the character limit I've just hit, but suffice to say; I'm warming to it, but I'm still deeply frustrated by very avoidable logic roadblocks and severe tech issues.  I stand by my original take - the joy and creativity of ES1 feels obfuscated by Fancy New Thing and "Graphics!!!!!!!!!"

comment_evidence.clause: music and animation are really good and I still enjoyed playing through it and would still recommend it but the game just felt like it was a major step down in a lot of ways compared to their last entry in the franchise
comment_evidence.full_review:
It's... okay? i guess

The map design barely feels like a metroidvania because of it's linearity and areas that don't really interconnect at all. The atmospheres of the areas in the game feel uninteresting and bland. 
The combat is fine but I hate the fact that attacking in a direction pushes you forward so much. All the bosses with the exception of maybe 2 are just way too uninspired and boring and don't really do that much until they just fall over and die. There isn't enough enemy variety, an area usually just has 3 types of enemies that spawn per room. Spawning the same easy boring enemies you've been fighting the entire game with triple the normal health and poise does not make it more engaging nor less boring. 
All the npc interactions and dialogue just don't really go anywhere and feel like there's something missing.

Other than that, the pixel art, music and animation are really good and I still enjoyed playing through it and would still recommend it but the game just felt like it was a major step down in a lot of ways compared to their last entry in the franchise.

comment_evidence.clause: backgrounds and animations all work really well on building the atmosphere together with great soundtracks you can hear as you explore the enviroment in the vicinity of Koho village and in the palace high above
comment_evidence.full_review:
Another installment of Momodora series. and another great game.

While not the longest, you can really feel the heart and effort the team put into the game, with little to no major bugs and quick patches fixing existing ones. Beautiful character graphics, backgrounds and animations all work really well on building the atmosphere together with great soundtracks you can hear as you explore the enviroment in the vicinity of Koho village and in the palace high above, as you uncover the mystery behind ringing of the bell.

Graphically an upgrade to previous installments, with only somewhat funky thing being character's spring animation (she swings her arms way too much) and double/wall jump (being just a 360 degree spin of character graphic). Apart from that everything is beautiful.

Audio is on really respectable level, both the background music, as the sounds of characters, hits and attack indicators.

The story is rather easy to follow and is not extremely complicated, but I think for Momodora it's a good thing. It wants to tell you a tale that you can be engaged in, myself I was really dragged into it, and was really thrilled and excited about what would happen next. 

Since the story is rather eqsy to follow you don't really need to wonder where you should go next, as it's both in dialogues and hints on the map rather clearly stated where you should no. With that said the game really rewards you for exploring since the very beginning, as it also shows rooms, where there is an item to collect, be it a stat up, a collectible fairy or a sigil.

Speaking of sigils, they are modifications to your character and you can equip up to 5 of them by the end of the game. There is quite a bit of them, some help you explore more smoothly, some are defence or offence focused, but pretty much all of them have some use, depending on what your needs or your playstyle are.

While the enemy variety is not the biggest, and some enemies are just copies of enemies from previous games, they usually pose a threat adequate to your progress when you meet them first.

For the last thing: special enemies, the so-called bosses. While there is quite a handful of them, almost none of them feel pointless or are boring to fight. There is maybe like 2 bad bosses in here, and final boss is not one of them, which is really great compared to previous installment. The final boss in this game is really engaging and while not the hardest of them all, he can pose quite a threat. Overall with the ending, I think he makes a satisfying finale for the game.

tl:dr Game good, graphics pretty, audio good, bosses fun, a little bit short. 8/10 from me, definitely worth the price.

comment_evidence.clause: The credits sequence with the screenshots and updated sprites for all the main characters of every game was also incredibly charming and cute and gave everything a great sense of finality
comment_evidence.full_review: The final entry in the Momodora series and honestly this is the best game of them all. Momo and Dora return from Momodora 3 for one new adventure together, an important relic has been stolen and thus the demons are returning wrecking havoc on the world and thus is up to Momo to find out what happened and saving the land. The first thing you notice about the game is how it looks, it's absolutely fantastic, every zone in this game is just stunning and the pixel art is incredibly expressive, accompany all this with the usual masterful soundtrack and you are already in for a great experience. Not only the world is more vibrant than before but there are a lot more of people to talk to, sidequests secrets to explore and the notes section also shine light on the timeline of events of the entire series and it felt rewarding for me after playing through the entire series. The credits sequence with the screenshots and updated sprites for all the main characters of every game was also incredibly charming and cute and gave everything a great sense of finality. The improvements are not only in the presentation the game takes everything Momodora Reverie Under the Moonlight did and just upgrades everything. The movement is better giving us a run button and a wall jump making exploration fun as hell, the pacing of the fights also got faster your attacks have more combo potential your dodge roll is also quicker and snappier. It still feels deliberate in the movement and as usual the bosses will deal a LOT of damage to you if you're not careful but this frantic rhythm gives us some of the best battles in the series. I don't know if we are ever getting a new Momodora game in the future, everything in this game makes it feel like this is the definitive end, but honestly this is probably the highest note the series ever reached so I can't think of a better way to go out. Check these games out all 5 of them, you won't regret it

comment_evidence.clause: The hit effects are a little lackluster (though to be fair technically the main weapon *is* just a leaf) but the rest of the present sound effects were satisfactory to me
comment_evidence.full_review:
C+ Beautiful game visually and musically but a step back to Reverie under the Moonlight (RutM) in terms of writing, level design, and gameplay.

Graphics : The strongest part of this game for me. I already loved the pixel art aesthetic of RutM and this game takes it to another level with much more fluid animation and detailed backgrounds. The characters all look amazing and the areas, while few, are varied and scenic. Bosses feature some lovely pixel art as well and are a definite upgrade.

Sound: The music is probably the second part of this game that I unequivocally enjoyed having several tracks that stood out for me and most of the other background osts feeling just right. The hit effects are a little lackluster (though to be fair technically the main weapon *is* just a leaf) but the rest of the present sound effects were satisfactory to me.

Plot: I enjoyed the general overt nature of the plot and progression in solving the mystery of the demon resurgence. However, I do think that it could have been better overall. I'll refrain from much criticism though due to the fact that this is my entry point into the mainline Momodora continuity (this game being the conclusion of the 4 game story to boot). The plot is simply written so that it's not a Herculean task to understand the basic of the story. But I definitely felt like I was missing some world building and story telling to help the writing solidify itself, though again it is highly possible that the legwork was accomplished in past 3 entries. My only point of reference here is via RuTM which served as a prequel to the series. At the end of that game the writing, while not masterful, displayed a competent level in drawing you into a world on the brink of ruin where most inhabitants have perished and those that remained on the brink of despair. At the end of the day I won't hold it against Momodora since I chose an entry point at the final hour but I certainly wasn't swayed by any of the developments that happened in this short adventure. It *is* a shame though that the loss of worldbuilding makes many of the bosses forgettable by the end of the game. While beautifully crafted, most end up being random characters slotted into the world because there needed to be boss fights. One of them is even just a giant blob, or another just a giant spider with basic designs on both. There isn't really any lore behind them so they end up being just another face in the crowd as opposed to RuTM where you end up fighting characters that mean something to the story like a Dark Souls for example.

Gameplay: The gameplay is adequate if somewhat stiff. The moveset is incredibly basic which to be fair is satisfactory given the short length of this adventure. Mainly just one string for the melee attack, bow and arrow, and a dodge. Later powerups include just the double jump and wall jump but ultimately you're trying to master the basic skillset to conquer bosses. I generally don't hold game accountable for a simple control scheme but in this case I feel it is a step back in their previous entry. My two main complaints are 1) RuTM has much more fluid dodge mechanics while Moonlit Farewell introduces a relatively frustrating amount of animation lock. It isn't abysmall levels of aniamtion lock but RuTM had such responsive control and feel that Moonlit Farewell is a clear stepback. 2) Also unlike RuTM, you cannot actually dodge in mid air in this game forcing awkward attempts to close in on ranged enemies situated on a high platform. Aside from player control the game also lacks real challenge. Regular enemies typically only have 1 move and are easily stunlocked by your melee combo. This makes traversal and combat somewhat boring as nearly every enemy can be negated by just hitting them first. Of the remaining enemy types, they typically follow the same behavior in that within a second or so they'll take a swing at you. Knowing this it is easy just to preemptively dodge and begin attacking at which point they will typically die before a second attack can come out. Bosses display similar lackluster behavior in that they are typically fairly easy to avoid and burst down in this game. Part of what made bosses of RuTM memorable was their difficulty. The game ultimately feels way to easy all around. I will give props to the team for the relics in this game since some of them are gameplay altering items in addition to the classic passive ones you'll see in many modern Metroidvanias. Collectibles are also easy to find, in a good way, and the map clearly defining boundaries and important landmarks.

Level design: The game is styled as a Metroidvania but unfortunately I think this entry is lacking, particularly in that it is a step back from RutM. RutM did not have the most amazing overworld compared to other metroidvanias but it did adequately in creating the interconnected world that you discovered as you obtained new powerups. Moonlit Farewell in contrast attempts to create a similar layout but lacks much of the openess and non-linearity of standard Metroidvanias, even compared to those that do a great deal of hand holding. The levels attempt to create an illusion of being open but by the end of the game it felt incredibly linear it its approach to exploration. This is further damning due to the fact that rooms are not particularly exciting in any capacity. Not really any puzzles, platforming challenges, interesting enemy placement, or even instant death traps that you have to watch out for. It leaves me somewhat dissappointed, though at the end of the day level design isn't really what I enjoyed the most out of RutM anyways.

comment_evidence.full_review:
This game is gorgeous, and as a fan of all the previous games I can say that it definitely lives up to the quality of previous instalments and then some. This game's fresh coat of paint is executed so perfectly, with barely any noticeable rough edges (an animation here and there is a little jank, but nothing major at all). The game felt floaty when I picked it up which I was nervous about, but it really suits the mechanics and style of gameplay they went for. Did I mention how good this game looks? Cause it looks really good. pretty short for the price, but the quality makes up for it tenfold. 
The soundtrack is BANGING especially in the latter half of the game, and omfg the final area's theme is SO SO SO GOOD (possibly better than pardoner's dance from RUtM????).
As a metroidvania, the exploration is very very solid, the size of the world makes backtracking not painful, and when it starts to get there BOOM they give you fast travel. The boss fights are all incredible, with my personal favourites being the recurring fights with the furry god and[spoiler]the fight against Dora after you beat the game.[/spoiler]
For people looking to get the most out of this game I would highly recommend playing the first two momodoras on Itch, then #3 and RUtM on steam before this one. It has a lot of cool callbacks to moments in the series that cant be appreciated unless you've played all of them, and they are great games in and of themselves.
I love this series with my whole ass heart, please give em a shot.

comment_evidence.full_review: Very well designed Metroidvania style game with a fantastic story and art design. Very high quality environments with amazing detail and plenty of care to make every area feel different and lively. The map design is less complex than other recent games in the genre like Bloodstained or Metroid Dread but makes good use of this simplicity to focus on preventing backtracking getting stale. Attacks and abilities feel very satisfying and progression is very smooth for the most part with only a minor drag between the mid to late game. This is excusable as the best abilities all come in the last section of the game. Bosses are all fun to fight and the inclusion of a Boss Rush mode is great, allowing me to go back and fight my favorite ones without having to start a new game just for that fight. My only gripes with Moonlit Farewell would be that it doesn't feel good to play on larger screens like a TV. With how the HUD moves to prevent being in the way of the player it means I may have to look much further down or up than I'd like to in order to get an idea of my current HP and MP when I'm in a fight. I'd say this game is best played on a 24 inch screen or smaller. The game also runs and feels great on the Steam Deck with it's smaller handheld size screen.

cases.case_title: 让漫画角色、笨重工业结构与警报光形成科幻恐怖语言

assessment.observation: 黄橙皮肤形成大体量，绿色龟壳、红发和黑色腕环构成分区；牙、爪、角和背刺反复表达危险，短粗躯干与大口部保留卡通夸张。官方线稿在不同视角下重复壳体、腹甲、腕环和尖刺。

cases.case_title: 用龟壳、尖刺和色块分区构成统一的反派角色符号

editorial_review.observation: 黄橙皮肤形成大体量，绿色龟壳、红发和黑色腕环构成分区；牙、爪、角和背刺反复表达危险，短粗躯干与大口部保留卡通夸张。官方线稿在不同视角下重复壳体、腹甲、腕环和尖刺。
editorial_review.comment: 值得借鉴的是有限符号的重复与族群规则统一。任天堂访谈记录了早期牛王联想、龟身与牛头的混合，以及与龟族共同线条的整理过程。知名度本身不作为视觉评分依据。
editorial_review.transfer: 设计强势角色时，可将体量、危险符号与主辅色绑定，再通过同族角色共享的结构规则维持世界观一致性。
editorial_review.limitations: 官方角色展示与设计访谈不等同于实机动作证据；未进行去 IP 识别测试。
